pretrial.name: Pretrial division
pretrial.description: Handles initial proceedings in criminal cases, such as bail hearings and applications for search warrants. This division also oversees some specialty programs, including the deferred prosecution court.

county.name: County division
county.description: Hears cases involving elections, adoptions, mental health proceedings, and real estate taxes.

law.name: Law division
law.description: Focuses on lawsuits for monetary damages larger than $30,000 in the city and larger than $100,000 in the suburbs. Examples of cases include personal injury, medical malpractice, and property damage.

assignment.name: Assignment
assignment.description: The Illinois Supreme Court can assign a circuit judge or retired judge to the appellate court for an indefinite term. There are currently nine Cook County circuit judges assigned to the appellate court.

first-municipal.name: First municipal district (Chicago)
first-municipal.description: This district handles felony preliminary hearings, misdemeanor cases, evictions, small claims, traffic, lawsuits seeking damages under $30,000, marriages, and civil unions within the city of Chicago.

juvenile-justice.name: Juvenile justice division
juvenile-justice.description: Conducts trials for minors charged with crimes and proceedings for minors addicted to alcohol or drugs and those who are runaways. Matters in this division are confidential.

reversal.name: Reversal
reversal.description: When a party in a court case believes the judge made the wrong decision, it can appeal to a higher court. If the higher court believes that the judge misapplied the law or abused their discretion, it can reverse the judge’s decision and send the case back with instructions. Usually cases get sent back to the same judge for corrections, but in rare circumstances higher courts order the cases to be transferred to a new judge.

associate-judge.name: Associate judge
associate-judge.description: These judges serve the same roles as circuit judges, but they are selected by a vote of the circuit judges, rather than by the public.

preliminary-hearing.name: Preliminary hearings
preliminary-hearing.description: Early hearings in criminal cases to determine whether arrested people will be incarcerated pre-trial and whether police had a right to make an arrest in the first place

criminal.name: Criminal division
criminal.description: Presides over felony cases, which are those that could result in a prison term of at least a year. This division also handles issues related to felony trials, including record expungement and petitions to review prior criminal convictions and sentences.

chancery.name: Chancery division
chancery.description: Handles lawsuits in which one party sues another to force them to stop or engage in a specific action. Cases involving mortgage foreclosures, contracts, and other matters are also heard here.

presiding-judge.name: Presiding judge
presiding-judge.description: Judges assigned by the chief judge to oversee administrative matters in each division and each municipal department. In some divisions, presiding judges are responsible for assigning cases to other judges. In other divisions, cases are assigned randomly by a computer. The presiding judges, along with Chief Judge Timothy Evans, are known as the Executive Committee and meet regularly to discuss courtwide matters.

domestic-violence.name: Domestic violence division
domestic-violence.description: Handles matters involving orders of protection, no-contact orders, and certain criminal cases related to domestic violence.

child-protection.name: Child protection division
child-protection.description: Hears cases involving child abuse and neglect, termination of parental rights, and orders of protection concerning children.

gal.name: Guardian ad litem
gal.description: An attorney appointed by the court to investigate and report to the court on the welfare and best interests of children, usually during domestic relations cases.

restorative-justice.name: Restorative justice community court
restorative-justice.description: Special courts for young adults ages 18-26 charged with nonviolent crimes aimed at rehabilitation and repairing harm. These courts use restorative justice principles, such as peace circles, reflection, and community involvement. Participants who successfully complete the program have their case dismissed and expunged.

probate.name: Probate division
probate.description: Hears matters involving wills, estates, and guardianship of minors and/or those with disabilities.

public-defender.name: Assistant public defender
public-defender.description: Attorneys who represent criminal defendants who cannot afford an attorney and parents accused by the state of child abuse or neglect.

states-attorney.name: Assistant state's attorney
states-attorney.description: Attorneys who prosecute state crimes in the county and represent county departments and officials in civil lawsuits.

specialty-courts.name: Problem-solving courts
specialty-courts.description: Special courts that combine intense supervision from a judge with services for people who committed non-violent crimes. Cook County has 20 problem-solving courts focused on drug treatment, mental health treatment, and veterans.

pro-se.name: Pro se
pro-se.description: Latin for “on one’s own behalf,” pro se litigants appear in court without an attorney. Although people charged in criminal court are entitled to an attorney, litigants in civil lawsuits and people challenging their criminal convictions are not always entitled to representation.

appointment.name: Appointment
appointment.description: When a judge resigns, retires, or is removed from office, it creates a vacancy on the court. The Illinois Supreme Court appoints a replacement to serve until the next election.

suburban-districts.name: Second through sixth municipal districts
suburban-districts.description: These suburban districts handle the same types of cases as the first district, but also oversee felony criminal cases and juvenile justice cases, orders of protection, some specialty courts, lawsuits seeking damages under $100,000, and name changes. These courts are located in Skokie, Rolling Meadows, Maywood , Bridgeview, and Markham.

post-conviction.name: Post-conviction
post-conviction.description: Petitions filed by someone who has already been convicted of a crime asking a judge to overturn their conviction or change their sentence. The bar for successfully filing a post-conviction petition is extremely high and usually requires petitioners to show they have access to new evidence that could not have been available to them at the time of the original trial. Post-conviction petitions are different from appeals, which focus narrowly on challenges to judges’ procedural decisions and interpretation of the law during a hearing or trial.

domestic-relations.name: Domestic relations division
domestic-relations.description: Hears cases involving divorce and family or child support matters.

administrative-law-judge.name: Administrative law judge
administrative-law-judge.description: Lawyers hired by city or state agencies to conduct hearings on administrative issues, such as municipal code violations or decisions made by agency representatives. May also be called “hearing officers.” These are not judicial positions but are often a stepping stone for attorneys who want to gain quasi-judicial experience before running for judge.

bench-book.name: Bench book
bench-book.description: A quick reference handbook that provides judges with an overview of procedural and evidence rules specific to the area of the law they’re tasked with applying in their courtroom. The book also guides judges in relevant legal precedent.

flags.name: Former prosecutor
flags.description: This candidate has served as a prosecutor in criminal or quasi-criminal cases at the city, county, state, or federal level.

flags.name: Notable controversy
flags.description: The candidate has been involved in some kind of personal or professional controversy. We report what we found in the “Notable” section and offer candidates an opportunity to respond to our reporting.

flags.name: Highly qualified ratings
flags.description: One or more bar associations have rated this candidate “well qualified” or “highly qualified.” Not all bar associations give out ratings higher than qualified. But those that do have suggested that this candidate is particularly well-qualified for retention.

retain-bertina-e-lampkin.judicialExperience: Lampkin was [appointed](#appointment) to the Illinois Appellate Court in 2009 and won election in 2016. She currently serves in the third division of the appellate court’s first district, hearing appeals out of Cook County. Before being appointed to the appellate court, she served for 22 years as a Cook County associate judge and circuit judge, including 12 years as a supervising judge in the [criminal division](#criminal).
retain-bertina-e-lampkin.pastExperience:
- Senior attorney, City of Chicago Law Department, defending the city against civil lawsuits (1985-1987) 
- Cook County [assistant state’s attorney](#states-attorney), prosecuting juvenile delinquency, sexual assault, and other felony cases (1974-1985)
retain-bertina-e-lampkin.notable:
Lampkin says she has written more than 400 opinions and orders as an appellate judge. In one recent example, she authored an opinion reversing the dismissal of a petition for [postconviction relief](#post-conviction) filed by a 51-year-old man sentenced to life in prison without the opportunity for parole for killing two teenagers in a gang-related fight when he was 18. In his petition, the man argued he was eligible for resentencing in light of state and U.S. Supreme Court decisions finding mandatory life without parole sentences for juveniles and young adults unconstitutional.

Lampkin has served on five different Illinois Supreme Court committees related to issues including capital cases, criminal law, and appellate court administration. To alleviate a backlog of criminal appeals, she spearheaded the creation of a group of pro bono attorneys to take on some of those cases. “In one year, 65 cases were disposed of,” Lampkin told Injustice Watch, including two murder convictions that were eventually tossed out, she said.

Lampkin was the lead prosecutor in the 1983 trial of Stanley Wrice, who was convicted in the brutal abduction and rape of a woman at his South Side home. Wrice was sentenced to 100 years in prison but was released in 2013 after a Cook County judge vacated his conviction based on Wrice’s claims that he was beaten into giving a statement by Chicago police lieutenants working under disgraced Cmdr. Jon Burge. Wrice’s case was significant in the Burge torture saga because it led the Illinois Supreme Court to establish that a confession coerced through torture must be thrown out, even if there is overwhelming evidence of a defendant’s guilt. Following his release, Wrice was denied a certificate of innocence, but he filed a federal civil rights lawsuit naming Lampkin as a defendant alongside Burge, his subordinates, and high-ranking law enforcement officials. The claims against Lampkin were dismissed, but she was made to sit for a deposition in 2016 and testify at the trial in 2020, records show. In her deposition, Lampkin was asked if she knew about the allegations of police torturing suspects on the South Side while she was a prosecutor. “Clearly some people were abused at Area 2, absolutely,” she said. “I don’t believe Stanley Wrice was.” In an interview with Injustice Watch, Lampkin continued to cast doubt on Wrice’s abuse claims and denied any wrongdoing. Wrice won a $5.2 million jury verdict against the city in March 2020.
retain-bertina-e-lampkin.surveyExcerpt: I saw the KKK burning a cross right off the highway and as a child, I watched TV with my parents as Rev. Dr. Martin Luther King, Jr. lead marches throughout the south, and I saw African American men, women and children have fire hoses turned on them or vicious dogs actually attack some of them. My father always told me that education was the key to changing the lives of Black people and I have strived all my life to be the best I could be in every endeavor.
retain-bertina-e-lampkin.ratingsExcerpt: The Chicago Council of Lawyers found Lampkin “meets, and exceeds, the higher standards that the Council uses in evaluating candidates for the Appellate Court.” The Illinois State Bar Association reports attorneys “speak highly of her knowledge and ability and her passion about the law” and that she is known to be “collegial, collaborative and gracious.”

survey.q: Where did you grow up and how has your personal background influenced your practice of law?
survey.a: I grew up on the south side of Chicago. My parents had 6 children. Every summer we would drive to Mississippi to visit my grandparents. There were places where my dad would not stop for gas in Illinois because of racism. When we got closer to Mississippi, I saw signs for restrooms and water fountains that said, “Whites Only,” “White Women Only,” “White Men Only,” or “Coloreds.” We never stopped for gas or to use these facilities. This was one way in which my dad taught me to have pride in who I was. I saw the KKK burning a cross right off the highway and as a child, I watched TV with my parents as Rev. Dr. Martin Luther King, Jr. lead marches throughout the south, and I saw African American men, women and children have fire hoses turned on them or vicious dogs actually attack some of them. My father always told me that education was the key to changing the lives of Black people and I have strived all my life to be the best I could be in every endeavor. I have done this in order to change the lives of Black people by continually stressing the importance of education and striving to be the best. My father told me that if I “was the best, white people, no matter how racist they were, would beat a path through the forest” in order to obtain my expertise. In every endeavor throughout my career, I have risen to the top and opened the door for other African Americans to enter.

survey.q: Judges hold enormous power over the lives of the people in their courtrooms. How have you grappled with judicial power in your time on the bench?
survey.a: I have always tempered justice with mercy. I have exercised extreme patience with litigants in front of me, especially with self-represented litigants and I have exercised my judicial power to treat people fairly in my courtroom. I do not allow one attorney to bully another in my courtroom, and I required everyone to be respectful to each other. For instance, I required all attorneys to call litigants and defendants by their proper name. I have always been a “second chance” judge. If, for instance, I could get someone to obtain their GED, I could convince the State’s Attorney’s Office to reduce or even sometimes drop their charge.

survey.q: As a judge, how have you worked, both inside and outside the courtroom, to address the ways that the legal system, historically and in the present, has worked in favor of those with money, power and resources and against those without?
survey.a:
Inside the courtroom I suggested to the Illinois Supreme Court to create a pro bono group of attorneys to help alleviate the backlog in the disposition of criminal appeals by the Office of the State Appellate Defender. The Supreme Court agreed, and the Committee I chair helps oversee the program. In one year, 65 cases were disposed of by these highly experienced and high-priced lawyers. In two cases I would like to highlight, the same pro bono firm received an outright reversal of a murder conviction for an indigent client. In another case a murder conviction was reversed and remanded for retrial. The same firm represented the accused on retrial and obtained a not guilty decision for the indigent defendant. I recognize that those who have power and money are on an uneven playing field with the poor and the powerless. Through the Committee I Chair, we work hand in hand with the Access to Justice Commission to assist the poor in achieving justice. 
** **
Outside the courtroom I have spoken at churches about the many contributions African Americans have made to the United States in almost every field of endeavor. I have spoken to “Just the Beginning – A Pipeline Organization” students of color, as well as pre-law summer programs for minority students at Chicago-Kent Law School and University of Illinois Chicago Law School, formally known as John Marshall Law School. 
** **
I have spoken to law students in celebration of Rev. Dr. Martin Luther King, Jr. Day. I have also shared my life story with hundreds of students to let them know that hard work, sacrifice and determination will allow them to reach their goals. 
** **
I am very proud of the work I have done with young African Americans. I have obtained summer employment for over 25 years for high school and college students in law firms, including Duane Morris LLP, Cooney & Conway, Cogan & Power, P.C., Power Rogers LLP, Clifford Law Offices PC, Romanucci & Blandin, LLC, and others. I have also hired four female African American law clerks and helped others obtain legal employment. I continue to work for diversity, equity, and inclusion of African Americans in the legal profession, and I have been a mentor to many young people of all ethnicities.
** **
I have participated in the Illinois Judicial Council’s food giveaway and clean water drives for low-income communities. I have financially supported the ACLU, NAACP, SPLC, and United Negro College Fund as well as donated to minority students through my law school. In addition, I have donated to Shriners Children’s Hospital, Lurie Children’s Hospital, St. Jude Children’s Hospital, Disabled American Veterans, Wounded Warriors, Doctors Without Borders, Pacific Garden Mission, the Greater Chicago Food Depository, as well as many others.

retain-kerry-m-kennedy.judicialExperience: Kennedy was elected to the circuit court in 2002. Since 2021, he has been the presiding judge of the [Bridgeview courthouse](#suburban-districts), where he has spent most of his judicial career hearing felony cases.
retain-kerry-m-kennedy.pastExperience: - Cook County [assistant public defender](#public-defender) at the Markham and Bridgeview courthouses (1979-2002)
retain-kerry-m-kennedy.notable:
During the past term, the Illinois Appellate Court has [reversed](#reversal) Kennedy’s dismissals of two postconviction petitions filed by men convicted of murder. One of the petitions was filed by Ricky Schoen, who was sentenced to 50 years in prison in 2014 for a gang-related drive-by shooting. Schoen, who claims he is innocent and had ineffective counsel, is asking for a new trial based on newly discovered evidence. The appellate court ordered Kennedy in 2022 to hold a hearing on his claims, and the case is ongoing.

In 2016, Kennedy increased the bond for an unemployed roofer from $2,000 to $50,000 without explanation after the man was charged with a DUI and battery against a police officer, the [Sun-Times reported](https://chicago.suntimes.com/2016/10/30/18352118/man-seeks-to-replace-hostile-judge-who-upped-bond-2-400). The appellate court later reduced the bond, a decision Kennedy sneered at in open court, prompting the defendant’s lawyer to file a motion to substitute Kennedy for another judge, the Sun-Times reported. Kennedy instead recused himself from the case, court records show.

Kennedy presided over a high-profile sexual assault trial in 2006 of one of several teenagers charged with raping a drunken 16-year-old girl and videotaping it. During the trial, Kennedy said he might hold the victim in contempt if she did not watch the video while on the witness stand, [according to the Chicago Tribune](https://www.chicagotribune.com/2006/03/02/judge-backs-down-in-rape-trial/). Defense attorneys had asked Kennedy to dismiss the charges if the girl would not watch it, arguing the defendant had a right to cross-examine his accuser. After an uproar from advocates, Kennedy the next day said he would not force the victim to watch the video, the Tribune reported.

Kennedy did not respond to requests for comment.
retain-kerry-m-kennedy.ratingsExcerpt: The Chicago Council of Lawyers said Kennedy is “doing a good job in his current assignment,” and the Illinois State Bar Association reported attorneys praised his legal knowledge and “ability to be pragmatic. He is considered to be well-prepared with high integrity.”

retain-joan-e-powell.judicialExperience: Powell was [appointed](#appointment) to the circuit court in 2006 and elected in 2008. She serves in the [law division](#law), where she presides over civil trials.
retain-joan-e-powell.pastExperience:
- Cook County [assistant state’s attorney](#states-attorney) in the complex litigation division, handling medical malpractice defense, employment and labor law, and civil rights matters (2000-2006)
- Law clerk for two Cook County circuit judges (1996-2000)
- Solo practitioner, focusing on contract, family, and elder law (1992-1996)
retain-joan-e-powell.notable:
The First District Appellate Court in 2025 sharply criticized Powell, [vacating a jury’s $43.8 million car crash verdict](https://law.justia.com/cases/illinois/court-of-appeals-first-appellate-district/2025/1-24-0220.html) against a trucking company and ordering that a new trial be held before a different judge, a rare move. The case involved a woman whose car had been rear-ended by a tractor-trailer while she was stopped at a traffic light, rendering her an incomplete quadriplegic.

In 2023, during jury selection in a trial over the amount of damages the company would have to pay, the woman’s attorneys published a blog post titled, “What Jurors Should Know But Don’t,” that said jurors were being “kept in the dark” about important case evidence. The next day, Powell collectively questioned the jurors about whether they’d seen the post, using leading statements the appellate court found “too suggestive toward a negative answer.” The appellate court said “any reasonable judge” would have taken the jurors aside one by one to learn whether they’d seen the posts.

Powell told Injustice Watch the language she used with jurors followed the Illinois Supreme Court jury instructions, but she has since started the practice of polling jurors one by one when issues arise. “We have higher courts for a good reason. It’s a double or triple check. This appellate court disagreed with me. It’s their job to review, and they did,” she said.
retain-joan-e-powell.ratingsExcerpt: The Illinois State Bar Association said Powell’s “legal knowledge, sensitivity to diversity, professionalism, impartiality, and temperament were excellent.” The Chicago Council of Lawyers reported that she’s known for her work ethic and good temperament.

retain-maureen-ward-kirby.judicialExperience: Kirby was [appointed](#appointment) to the circuit court in 2007 and elected the following year. Since 2023, Kirby has been the [presiding judge](#presiding-judges) of the [county division](#county), where she has heard cases since 2009. retain-maureen-ward-kirby.pastExperience: - Associate and partner at a Chicago-based law firm, handling commercial litigation cases (1989-2008)
retain-maureen-ward-kirby.notable: Kirby currently presides over a lawsuit filed in 2024 by the nonprofit Reform for Illinois to force the Cook County clerk to allow the City of Evanston to hold ranked-choice voting, following a referendum on the issue that passed by a wide margin in 2022. Kirby [dismissed the lawsuit in November 2024](https://www.chicagotribune.com/2024/11/27/cook-county-judge-scraps-ranked-choice-voting-set-to-start-in-evanston-in-2025/) after the county clerk argued it couldn’t administer ranked-choice elections without state officials first authorizing those types of elections. The Illinois Appellate Court ordered Kirby to reopen the case in 2025, ruling that no substantive rulings could be made because the City of Evanston was not a party to the lawsuit. Earlier this year, Reform for Illinois and the city refiled the lawsuit, adding the state board of elections and Dominion Voting Systems as defendants. Their attorney [told the Evanston RoundTable](https://evanstonroundtable.com/2026/08/13/ranked-choice-voting-suit-reset-again-to-loop-in-state-election-board-voting-machine-vendor/) they expect Kirby to issue a ruling before Evanston’s upcoming special mayoral election, with a primary likely to be held in February.
retain-maureen-ward-kirby.ratingsExcerpt: The Chicago Council of Lawyers found Kirby qualified but did not explain why. The Illinois State Bar Association said lawyers praised her “integrity, even-handedness and ability to handle a variety of legal issues.”

retain-edward-a-arce.judicialExperience: Arce was [appointed](#appointment) to the circuit court in 2008 and won election later the same year from the 14th Subcircuit. He currently hears cases in the [domestic relations division](#domestic-relations).
retain-edward-a-arce.pastExperience: - Associate and partner at a small firm, handling a variety of civil cases, including family law, bankruptcy, and contract disputes (1985-2008)
retain-edward-a-arce.notable:
Arce is currently presiding over a parentage case filed in 2019 by then-59-year-old Daryl Miller, who is seeking to establish that blues musician Buddy Guy is his biological father. Miller filed his petition after Guy voluntarily took a genetic test that established that Guy couldn’t be excluded as the father. After the Illinois Appellate Court [reversed](#reversal) Arce’s [decision to dismiss the case](https://law.justia.com/cases/illinois/court-of-appeals-first-appellate-district/2023/1-21-0774.html), he ordered Guy to submit to a new paternity test in July.

Arce’s family owns Tropical Optical, a retail eyewear and optometry chain started by his father, and Sun Optics, an eyewear manufacturing company in which Arce is a shareholder. Arce said he draws no income from the businesses. The family has also been active in local politics, including through a now-defunct political action committee, the Mexican American PAC, which was managed by his brother Daniel between 1989 and 2019 and backed politicians allied with Mayor Richard M. Daley and disgraced former Ald. Ed Burke.
retain-edward-a-arce.ratingsExcerpt: Most lawyers interviewed by the Chicago Council of Lawyers described Arce as “an excellent judge,” however some reported that he “can be so procedurally driven that he misses opportunities to resolve cases early.” Attorneys who spoke with the Illinois State Bar Association said he is “diligent and prompt.”

retain-thomas-j-byrne.judicialExperience: Byrne hears [criminal cases](#criminal) at the Leighton Criminal Courthouse in Chicago. He previously handled misdemeanor cases in Chicago.
retain-thomas-j-byrne.pastExperience: - Cook County [assistant state’s attorney](#states-attorney) serving at courthouses in Chicago and Markham, eventually rising to supervisor at the Rolling Meadows courthouse (1989-2008)
retain-thomas-j-byrne.notable:
The Illinois Appellate Court has overturned Byrne’s judgments, rulings, or sentences at least 16 times over the last term, the second-highest number among the six criminal division judges up for retention this year, though far fewer than [some judges](https://www.injusticewatch.org/project/2022/charles-burns-reversed-decisions-retention/) running [in past elections](https://www.injusticewatch.org/judges/judicial-elections/2018-retention/2018/chicago-harshest-judge-seeks-retention/). Some [reversals](#reversal) stemmed from the mistakes of defense attorneys or extraordinarily technical legal questions. In several others, the appeals court found he too quickly rejected people challenging their convictions.

In one case last year, the appellate court [criticized Byrne’s decision](https://law.justia.com/cases/illinois/court-of-appeals-first-appellate-district/2025/1-23-1679.html) to prevent a jury from seeing police body camera video showing a witness giving statements that might have bolstered a defendant’s self-defense claim in a 2020 brawl in Chicago. The witness, a 90-year-old man, testified at trial that he wasn’t sure whether the defendant or an alleged victim threw the first punch. The defendant’s attorney sought to counter that testimony by showing the jury video of him telling a police officer at the scene that the first thing he saw was the alleged victim punching her and “beating that woman like she was a dog.” After watching the video in his chambers, Byrne said the recorded statements were improper hearsay and barred them. The jury convicted the defendant of aggravated battery, and the judge sentenced her to 2½ years in prison. The appellate court reversed her conviction, saying Byrne should have let the jury see the video since it contradicted the testimony the witness gave in court. The case is still pending.

Byrne declined to comment through a spokesperson.
retain-thomas-j-byrne.ratingsExcerpt: The Illinois State Bar Association said Byrne is respected by prosecutors and defense attorneys alike and praised for his fairness. The Chicago Council of Lawyers reported appreciation for his courtroom management and his “low-key, effective demeanor.”

retain-diana-l-kenworthy.judicialExperience: Kenworthy handles [felony criminal trials](#criminal) at the Leighton Criminal Courthouse in Chicago. She previously served in the [domestic violence division](#domestic-violence) and heard misdemeanor cases in the [first municipal district](#first-municipal).
retain-diana-l-kenworthy.pastExperience:
- Partner at a small family firm, arbitrator for the circuit court, and hearing officer for the Metropolitan Water Reclamation District (2000-2008)
- Cook County [assistant public defender](#public-defender) (1996-2000)
retain-diana-l-kenworthy.notable:
In 2022, Kenworthy acquitted Jimmy Jackson in the murder of his on-and-off girlfriend, Daisy Hayes, citing a lack of physical evidence and saying video of him leaving her apartment with a suitcase he threw in the trash did not clearly establish guilt. Kenworthy said Hayes appeared intoxicated the day she was last seen and cited medications on her nightstand in finding there was reasonable doubt that Jackson killed her. Hayes’ body was never found.

“I know that my ruling will be difficult and frustrating for Ms. Hayes’ family,” the judge said in delivering her verdict. “I want to be clear: My finding is not that Mr. Jackson is innocent, rather my finding is that the state is not able to meet the very high burden of proving the defendant guilty of the charges beyond a reasonable doubt.”

Hayes’ family members [held a press conference after the verdict](https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2022/4/26/23043130/daisy-hayes-judge-diana-kenworthy-campaign-justice-murder-not-guilty), and they continue to criticize Kenworthy years later. “As a Black woman, it just makes you feel that the system, the justice system, doesn’t care about us,” Teresa Smith, her daughter, told Injustice Watch recently. 

Kenworthy declined to comment through a spokesperson.

survey.q: Where did you grow up and how has your personal background influenced your practice of law?
survey.a:
I was born and raised in Columbus, Ohio. I attended The Ohio State University for undergrad, and moved to Chicago for law school. Chicago very quickly felt like home. I realized I wanted to give back to this city that I love and that has shaped how I approach the bench more than any single course in law school. I came to law through a non-traditional path; I have a Bachelor of Science in Natural Resources Development from Ohio State and worked in environmental consulting before my J.D. from Chicago-Kent. My earlier training taught me to think in terms of systems: how one intervention ripples through an ecosystem, how “right plant, right place” matters as much as good intentions. I bring that same lens to the courtroom. A person in front of me is not a discrete legal problem to be resolved but someone embedded in a family, a neighborhood, a community, and a set of circumstances that a single ruling can't rewrite on its own.
I also bring decades of personal family experience with the kinds of struggles—mental health, substance use, trauma—that show up daily in my courtroom. While I don’t lead with that from the bench, it is part of why I sought out problem-solving courts (Mental Health Court and Veterans Treatment Court) rather than staying on a general docket. I've spent my judicial career trying to be the difference between mere punishment and helping someone get the resources they need to address the underlying problems that have brought them into the criminal justice system in the first place.

survey.q: Judges hold enormous power over the lives of the people in their courtrooms. How have you grappled with judicial power in your time on the bench?
survey.a:
I've been on the bench since December 2008, and the longer I sit, the more I think my answer is: carefully and never comfortably. Problem-solving courts make that power especially visible. In Mental Health Court and Veterans Treatment Court, I'm not just deciding guilt or a sentence; I'm making weekly decisions that shape whether someone stays housed, keeps a job, stays connected to treatment, or ends up back in custody. That's a different role than the typical general docket, and I don't think it's possible to hold it responsibly without constant self-scrutiny.
Concretely, means following consistent guidelines and practices to ensure everyone appearing is treated fairly and impartially. We use phase progression charts, consistent check-in protocols, documented criteria, so that my discretion is channeled rather than unbounded. I have also pursued formal training in addiction, psychology, Motivational Interviewing and relational skills, because the tone and posture I bring to a status hearing influences outcomes. Good intentions are not a substitute for training and skill. Finally, my role in problem-solving courts works best when participants experience me less as someone who can punish them and more as someone who is genuinely tracking their progress and celebrating their successes while still holding them accountable along the path.
I have to grapple with the discomfort of how much a person's future can turn on decisions made in a short hearing. I am an advocate for a Problem-Solving Courts Division, better relationships with the Public Defender’s Office and State’s Attorneys, all so that outcomes are based less on the individual judge one appears before and on defensible, consistent standards.

survey.q: As a judge, how have you worked, both inside and outside the courtroom, to address the ways that the legal system, historically and in the present, has worked in favor of those with money, power and resources and against those without?
survey.a:
Inside the courtroom, my primary tool has been the problem-solving court model itself. Problem-solving courts create an alternative track for non-violent offenders who face issues from untreated mental illness, substance use, or the aftermath of military service; rather than requiring them to have the resources to solve those problems before the court will treat them fairly, problem-solving courts strive to help provide those resources. I have worked to develop participant-facing materials built around executive functioning, coping skills, and financial stability, in clear and plain language, to help participants in their journey. Equal treatment under the law means nothing if the materials explaining the justice system and the path through problem-solving courts are inaccessible to a participant. I also worked on the Restorative Justice Community Court, which strives to bring restorative justice to Chicago communities as a means to move beyond simple punishment for non-violent offenders and to heal the relationships in communities that can be the root cause of some types of crime.
Outside the courtroom, I've spent over ten years supporting and promoting Problem-Solving Courts in Cook County. Often, the people most burdened by an under-resourced system are the ones with the least ability to advocate for its reform themselves. Though much of the work must be done at a legislative level, there are appropriate avenues for judges to advocate for judicial reform and I believe restorative justice and problem-solving courts represent how the Judicial branch can offer solutions to improve the status quo for all communities.

retain-ursula-walowski.notable:
The First District Illinois Appellate Court overturned Walowski’s judgments, rulings, or sentences at least 25 times over her most recent six-year term, sometimes in pointed language. That’s more than any other criminal court judge seeking retention this year, though fewer than some [other judges](https://www.injusticewatch.org/judges/judicial-elections/2018-retention/2018/chicago-harshest-judge-seeks-retention/) [in past years](https://www.injusticewatch.org/project/2022/charles-burns-reversed-decisions-retention/). Some of the appellate rulings stemmed from technical errors or failures by defense attorneys, but the court directly criticized her work repeatedly. In [one case](https://law.justia.com/cases/illinois/court-of-appeals-first-appellate-district/2024/1-22-1875.html), appellate judges [reversed](#reversal) Walowski’s guilty verdict at a bench trial and said the evidence simply was not strong enough to convict.

In 2021, [an appellate panel ruled unanimously](http://illinoiscourts.gov/R23_Orders/AppellateCourt/2021/1stDistrict/1171721_R23.pdf) that Walowski should not have forced an attorney to go forward with a trial in 2017 over his repeated objections that he couldn’t properly defend his client as he was recovering from food poisoning and its aftereffects. The attorney, Bernard Shelton Jr., asked Walowski for time to recover after he’d gone to the emergency room the previous day with a swollen face, but she rejected him, saying he “did a fine job” despite his complaints earlier in the trial. Appellate Court Judge Mary L. Mikva wrote that Walowski abused her discretion and denied the defendant a fair trial by brushing aside Shelton’s complaints. 

In 2023, Appellate Court Judge Bertina Lampkin [wrote a unanimous ruling](https://law.justia.com/cases/illinois/court-of-appeals-first-appellate-district/2023/1-21-0912.html) criticizing Walowski for failing to explain the constitutional right to an attorney or the potential consequences of representing himself to a murder defendant, Wynton Stewart, who then disastrously acted as his own lawyer and was convicted. The appellate judges called Walowski’s work “a complete failure” to follow rules intended to guarantee Stewart a fair trial and reversed his conviction. Stewart was later convicted again.

Walowski told Injustice Watch she thinks the reversals stem in part from her working efficiently through a high volume of cases in criminal court, where cases are frequently appealed. She declined to comment on specific cases, in keeping with court rules, but said, “I respect the appellate court’s decisions.”

“I do try to get things right as much as possible in each particular case, but sometimes things can be missed,” she said. “Mistakes can happen, but I strive to avoid them.”
retain-ursula-walowski.ratingsExcerpt: “Despite comments about poor temperament and impatience, Judge Walowski was praised for her legal knowledge, her willingness to research, and her courtroom management ability,” said the Illinois State Bar Association. The Chicago Council of Lawyers said that although some lawyers reported her “treating attorneys and litigants harshly, most said they were willing to deal with her impatience and flare-ups because of what a reasonable and knowledgeable jurist she is.”

retain-caroline-kate-moreland.notable:
Moreland’s appointment to the bench played a role in the 2023 federal corruption trial of disgraced former Chicago Ald. Ed Burke. Prosecutors accused Burke of holding up the renovation of the city’s massive Old Main Post Office until the developer hired Burke’s law firm to handle its property tax appeals on the building. In a secretly recorded meeting with the developer, Burke dangled his relationship with Moreland’s father, then-Amtrak board vice-chairman Jeffrey Moreland, when discussing the challenges getting the railroad company to stop its trains from running under the building for the renovation to start. “We made his daughter a judge here in Cook County. … We’re family personal friends,” Burke says in the video from October 2016 played in court, according to news reports. Burke’s wife, Anne M. Burke, sat on the Illinois Supreme Court when it appointed Moreland to the bench. Burke was convicted in December 2023 of racketeering, bribery, and attempted extortion, and sentenced to two years in prison, plus a $2 million fine. A spokesperson for the Illinois Supreme Court refused to say whether or not the court investigated Burke’s comments. Emails to Ed Burke’s attorneys went unanswered. Moreland declined to comment.

Moreland was one of three judges who dropped out of primary races against candidates favored by the Cook County Democratic Party in 2012, only to be reappointed after the election by the state Supreme Court, [the Chicago Tribune reported](https://www.chicagotribune.com/2012/12/23/defeated-judges-find-way-back-to-bench-2/). By dropping out, Moreland cleared the field for Michael T. Mullen, who’s currently the chancery division’s presiding judge. “I didn’t make any deals,” Moreland told the Tribune about her decision to withdraw from the race. “That was a personal and political decision that I made.”

Several of Moreland’s rulings in the past term have made the news. In September 2020, Moreland dismissed a lawsuit seeking class-action status against the city of Chicago for issuing thousands of Central Business District parking tickets to people who weren’t parked there, saying the plaintiff had failed to exhaust the administrative appeals process; the Illinois Supreme Court upheld her ruling. In 2025, Moreland [ordered former Orland Park Mayor Keith Pekau](https://southwestregionalpublishing.com/2025/08/15/judge-orders-pekau-to-take-down-confidential-village-records/) to take down confidential information about the village he had posted online after he lost re-election; the case remains ongoing. Also in 2025, Moreland granted class-action status to[ a lawsuit filed by a resident on Chicago’s East Side](https://www.chicagotribune.com/2026/08/19/southeast-side-pollution-odors-landfill-fires/) against an animal feed plant for blanketing the neighborhood in noxious odors. The Illinois Attorney General’s Office later filed its own lawsuit against the plant.
retain-caroline-kate-moreland.ratingsExcerpt: The Illinois State Bar Association said Moreland is “fair to everyone, and considerate of pro se litigants.”

survey.q: Where did you grow up and how has your personal background influenced your practice of law?
survey.a: I grew up on the southside of Chicago in a working class/ blue collar neighborhood. My father was a fireman and my mother was a stay at home mom taking care of six children, one of which was a down syndrome child. I learned so much watching and learning from my mother and other mothers of down syndrome children. My mother and other courageous mothers fought for proper care and respect for down syndrome children. They were trail blazers who helped children with developmental disabilities. Helping my mom with my brother and witnessing first hand the compassion and love for him gave me a great understanding of special needs children at an early age. I carried these values during my legal career and on the bench, showing compassion and understanding for everyone. To this day I feel a great sense of belonging to help those in need. My neighborhood roots – being surrounded by hardworking, loving and caring people are with me each day I serve on the bench. I continue to help my mom take care of my down syndrome brother, and that in turn constantly reminds me of what is really important – compassion and understanding.

survey.q: Judges hold enormous power over the lives of the people in their courtrooms. How have you grappled with judicial power in your time on the bench?
survey.a: I have never really thought of myself as having judicial power. If we do have power, then I would define that power as the duty and responsibility to apply the law evenly and fairly to the people we serve each day in our courtrooms. That means understanding the law and applying it consistently based on the facts and circumstances before us. This requires that we listen and truly hear what the parties appearing before us are really saying. Once we understand this, the backstory of what happened to each person who appears before us becomes clearer and that allows us to render a decision on what really happened in the case before us. Our next responsibility is then to fully explain to the parties why we ruled as we did. The people we serve deserve to understand why we decided a particular way. Lastly, we have the responsibility to control the decorum in our courtroom so that everyone is treated with the utmost respect throughout the proceeding which is manifested in our temperament in the courtroom. I always try to ease their anxiety by keeping everyone calm by creating an atmosphere in the courtroom where everyone feels comfortable. Judicial power is really a judicial responsibility to everyone to do the right thing under the law in the right manner consistently.

survey.q: As a judge, how have you worked, both inside and outside the courtroom, to address the ways that the legal system, historically and in the present, has worked in favor of those with money, power and resources and against those without?
survey.a: Judges should do their best to address gaps in our legal system in the way it may favor those with money over those with less means. People with less means to support themselves sometimes need help from us. As a judge I feel I can be the equalizer for them. For example, excessive fines and costs put the less fortunate in an impossible situation. I always do my best to help ease this financial burden by vacating their fines and costs when a hardship exists. This could help avoid the collateral consequences caused by the nonpayment of fines and costs such as driver’s license suspensions and judgments/collections. I also make sure everyone is aware of legal resources that are available. I appoint legal counsel. I also direct those of less means to outside resources to help them.

He shouldn’t know about court dates.” A federal judge dismissed the suit, ruling that Romanek was “entitled to absolute judicial immunity” and pointing to a U.S. Supreme Court decision establishing that “trial judges have wide latitude to control courtroom atmosphere and litigants who appear before them.” Paris has an appeal pending before the 7th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals.

In a written statement, Romanek did not address Paris’ lawsuit directly, but said “I consider the best interest of the children of my litigants first and foremost. This includes keeping children from the courtroom who are not litigants and should not be testifying against family members. In decision making, I rely on the law and the evidence as well as experts such as [guardians ad litem](#gal) and mental health professionals.”

Attorneys who spoke with Injustice Watch described Romanek as curt and easily annoyed, and some said she appeared unprepared for hearings and sometimes delayed cases unnecessarily. Nevertheless, most attorneys described her as fair, knowledgeable about the law, and reasonable in her decisions. The attorneys spoke on condition of anonymity because they have cases before her.

“I sit in a very volatile courtroom,” Romanek said in her statement. “All the litigants involved in domestic relations cases are angry and unhappy. Thus it is not surprising that some people are unhappy with the end result of their cases. Nevertheless, I take my role in the judiciary extremely seriously. I prepare for all of my cases prior to hearing. I also maintain a judicial demeanor at all times. If I find myself getting agitated, I take a break from the courtroom and walk for a few minutes.”

The Illinois Appellate Court [last year overturned Coughlin’s 38-year prison sentence](https://docs.publicnow.com/viewDoc?filename=113919%5CEXT%5CDD96857ECC6253F8C3DB4C32FC42D1FA048656AA_11F0EF6A54452362D12CFC0C9655BD2AB1D01C98.PDF) for Lavert Bonner, who shot and killed Lawrence Mack in Markham in 2010 when Bonner was 17. Coughlin had heard testimony and seen evidence that Bonner acted in self-defense after a childhood of neglect and instability, and he noted in court that Bonner had potential to be rehabilitated. Appellate Court Judge Ramon Ocasio III wrote for the majority that Coughlin abused his discretion, saying his explanation of the sentence didn’t justify its length. “Given the court’s express finding that Bonner has rehabilitative potential, we do not understand why or how it concluded that the appropriate sentence was one that, if served in full, will keep Bonner in prison until he is 55½ years old,” Ocasio wrote.

Appellate Court Judge Mary K. Rochford dissented, suggesting her colleagues were improperly second-guessing Coughlin based on their own judgment of the case. Citing court rules, Coughlin told Injustice Watch he couldn’t comment on a pending case. 

Bonner, who turns 34 in October, has yet to be resentenced. He wrote a letter to the court asking for a shorter term and saying, “I was 17 years old when I made the most terrible mistake of my life. … I wish I could take it all back.”

survey.q: Where did you grow up and how has your personal background influenced your practice of law?
survey.a:
I grew up in Calumet Park and continue to reside in the south suburbs of Cook County. I attended Loyola University, where I met my wife of 33 years, and I attended DePaul College of Law in the evenings while working full-time during the day. In 2014, after working for 18 years with the Cook County State’s Attorney’s Office, I was elected as a Circuit Court Judge in the 15th Judicial Subcircuit of Cook County. 
Regardless of personal background, according to the Judicial Code of Conduct, a judge must interpret and apply the law without regard to whether the judge approves or disapproves of the law in question. Over the last 12 years as a judge, I have strived to be impartial and fair to all parties, and I believe those efforts contributed to every reviewing bar associations’ recommendation that I be retained as a judge in 2020.

survey.q: Judges hold enormous power over the lives of the people in their courtrooms. How have you grappled with judicial power in your time on the bench?
survey.a: I believe that humility, patience, and respect for everyone you interact with are essential for maintaining a good judicial temperament. I always try to remember that what may be a routine court appearance for attorneys, can be a very confusing and stressful event for those unfamiliar with criminal proceedings. As a result, I always try to explain what is happening -- why a continuance is being given, why I am ruling a certain way -- so that even if a party does not agree with the decision, they will know why the ruling was made.

survey.q: As a judge, how have you worked, both inside and outside the courtroom, to address the ways that the legal system, historically and in the present, has worked in favor of those with money, power and resources and against those without?
survey.a: Discrimination and bias, whether based on race, gender, sexual orientation, ethnicity, religion, or socio-economic status have no place in a court of justice. I strive every day to hear the matters before me fairly and impartially. According to the _Illinois Code of Judicial Conduct_, “An independent judiciary requires that judges decide cases according to the law and facts, without regard to whether particular laws or litigants are popular or unpopular with the public, the media, government officials, or the judge’s friends or family. Confidence in the judiciary is eroded if judicial decision making is perceived to be subject to inappropriate outside influences.” Judges must follow the law, even when doing so is against the popular will of the time. Regardless of public sentiment, a judge must only adhere to the laws, to judicial precedents, and to the constitution.

retain-megan-elizabeth-goldish.notable:
Since her retention in 2020, Goldish has had to answer questions under oath about her role in the separate wrongful prosecutions of John Velez and Omar Williams. As a felony review prosecutor, Goldish approved murder charges against Velez in 2001 and Williams in 2011. Velez was convicted but [ultimately exonerated in 2017](https://www.injusticewatch.org/judges/judicial-elections/2020-retention/2020/judge-goldish-velez-case/), after his girlfriend recanted a statement she gave to police, saying it was coerced. Williams was [incarcerated pretrial for more than five years and eight months](https://www.injusticewatch.org/criminal-courts/prosecutors/2017/five-years-of-waiting-in-jail-then-a-quick-jury-acquittal/) before a jury acquitted him, also in 2017. In both cases, key witnesses said statements prepared by Goldish contained falsehoods and they were made to sign the statements under duress, according to federal civil rights lawsuits filed by Velez and Williams. Federal judges in both lawsuits allowed claims against Goldish to proceed, and she was made to sit for hours-long depositions in each case and to testify in court during Willliams’ civil trial, records show. Williams’ attorneys eventually voluntarily dismissed the claims against Goldish, and a jury awarded Williams $100,000 in damages in 2021. Velez settled his lawsuit against Goldish and the county in 2024 for $2.4 million.

In an email, Goldish downplayed her role in both prosecutions. “These matters are approximately 20 years old and my involvement in each was peripheral,” she said. “There has never been any finding that I engaged in misconduct.”

Goldish has long been a prolific donor in Cook County politics. Since becoming a judge, she’s made more than 150 donations for a total of about $74,000, including dozens of donations to judicial candidates, records show. In an email, Goldish said the “overwhelming majority” of her contributions were tickets she purchased for fundraising events “involving friends, colleagues, and people with whom I have worked over many years.”

Goldish is married to Matthew Savage, a Chicago police sergeant. Two cases Goldish handled in recent years involving Chicago police have made the news. In August, Goldish granted an emergency order of protection for [a woman who alleged she had been beaten and held against her will by her boyfriend](https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/08/21/chicago-police-cpd-vecchio-snelling), Chicago police officer Joseph Vecchio, records show. Vecchio was ordered detained at Cook County Jail by another judge a day later. In 2019, Goldish [dismissed a misdemeanor domestic battery charge](https://www.chicagotribune.com/2019/08/16/chicago-cop-on-mayor-lightfoots-security-detail-cleared-of-misdemeanor-domestic-battery-charge/) against a police officer on former Mayor Lori Lightfoot’s security detail. The officer was accused by her ex-girlfriend of pushing her and pinning her against the wall of their home. Goldish sided with the accused, citing surveillance footage that didn’t show any physical altercation and noting the accuser took three days to report the incident to police, which Goldish said was “very telling,” according to the Chicago Tribune.

survey.q: Where did you grow up and how has your personal background influenced your practice of law?
survey.a:
I grew up in Skokie, an incredibly diverse community. While known for its sizable Jewish population, including many Holocaust survivors, Skokie has always been home to vibrant immigrant communities from around the world. I grew up with classmates and friends whose families came from many different nations, practiced several different faiths, and spoke many different languages. My high school was one of the most diverse in the nation in terms of the languages spoken and the faith traditions represented. Diversity was not something I learned about in a textbook, as it was simply the community in which I was raised. It was a wonderful and unique place to grow up, and I am proud that my hometown continues to grow more diverse with each passing year.
Growing up surrounded by Holocaust survivors left a lasting impression on me. Their stories were a constant reminder of the consequences of hatred, prejudice, and indifference, and of the critical importance of the rule of law, equal justice, and protecting the rights of every person. Those lessons shaped not only my worldview but also my understanding of what our legal system should strive to achieve.
Living in such a diverse community also gave me an early appreciation for the challenges many immigrant families face. I saw firsthand how language barriers, unfamiliarity with government systems, economic hardship, and cultural differences could make it difficult to access services, navigate the legal system, or seek help. I also came to understand the isolation and emotional strain that can accompany starting over in a new country.
Those experiences influenced my decision to become a lawyer and continue to shape my work today. I knew that when I became a lawyer, I wanted to help ensure that people from all backgrounds were treated equally – that immigrant families from Skokie had the same access to services and protection as those from more privileged backgrounds. My entire legal career has been in public service. As a sitting judge in the Domestic Violence Division, I strive to ensure that every person who enters my courtroom is treated with dignity, fairness, and respect, regardless of their background, language, culture, religion, or immigration status. I recognize that for many litigants, the courthouse can be an intimidating place, particularly for those who have experienced trauma or who are unfamiliar with our legal system.
Throughout my career, I have been passionate about improving access to justice and educating diverse communities about domestic violence protections and available resources. On the bench, I work to ensure that meaningful language access, high-quality interpreter services, trauma-informed practices, and appropriate community resources are available so that every individual has a fair opportunity to be heard. The values I learned growing up in Skokie- that diversity is a strength, that the rule of law matters, and that justice must be accessible to everyone—continue to guide me every day.

survey.q: Judges hold enormous power over the lives of the people in their courtrooms. How have you grappled with judicial power in your time on the bench?
survey.a:
In the Domestic Violence Courthouse, we deal with incredibly difficult cases and subjects. I am cognizant of the life-altering nature of many decisions we must make and the impact they have not just on individuals but on children, families and the entire community. Serving as a judge has reinforced for me that judicial power is not just a privilege: it is a profound public trust.
Every day, I make decisions that can dramatically affect the lives of the people who appear before me. Those decisions can determine whether someone is a risk to commit violence in the future, whether a family member is protected by an order of protection, whether a parent can have contact with a child, or whether a criminal conviction will alter the course of a person's future. I have never lost sight of the weight of that responsibility. I treat everyone who comes before me fairly, equally and with respect - and with recognition of the fact that even being in my courtroom can be a deeply traumatic experience.   
As a judge in the Domestic Violence Division, I preside over some of the most difficult and emotionally charged cases in our justice system. The issues before the court often involve allegations of violence between family members or intimate partners, trauma, mental health concerns, substance abuse, children, housing, immigration consequences, and financial instability. 
Because of that, I approach every case with humility. I recognize that I see people at some of the worst moments of their lives. Whether a person is a victim seeking protection, a defendant facing criminal charges, or a family member caught in the middle of a painful dispute, everyone who enters my courtroom deserves to be heard, treated with dignity, and afforded the full protections of due process. I strive to ensure that every litigant believes they had a meaningful opportunity to tell their story and that my decisions are based on the evidence and the law, not assumptions, emotion, or personal opinion.
I am particularly mindful of the extraordinary authority judges possess when making decisions about future risk. Determining whether someone poses a danger to another person, whether contact between family members should be restricted, or whether conditions of release are necessary requires careful judgment. These decisions are among the most consequential a judge can make, and they demand both compassion and discipline. My responsibility is not to predict the future with certainty, but to faithfully apply the law to the facts presented, recognizing both the need to protect victims and the constitutional rights of those accused.
Grappling with judicial power also means recognizing its limits. A judge cannot solve every problem that appears in a courtroom. Many of the underlying issues that bring people before the court such as poverty, addiction, untreated mental illness, intergenerational trauma, or lack of resources, cannot be resolved by a judicial order alone. What I can do is ensure that every person is treated fairly, that proceedings are conducted with integrity, and that litigants are connected with appropriate services and resources whenever possible.
Ultimately, I believe the proper exercise of judicial power begins with humility. The position is a reminder not of authority for its own sake, but of an obligation to exercise that authority thoughtfully, impartially, and with respect for the humanity of every person who comes before the court. If people leave my courtroom believing they were heard, treated with dignity, and judged fairly according to the law, then I have fulfilled one of the most important responsibilities entrusted to me.

survey.q: As a judge, how have you worked, both inside and outside the courtroom, to address the ways that the legal system, historically and in the present, has worked in favor of those with money, power and resources and against those without?
survey.a:
In addition to my daily work to ensure everyone in my courtroom has equal access to both services and fundamental justice, I have been involved in a wide variety of initiatives to help communities that have suffered discrimination in the legal system and in society at large. The legal system functions best when every person, regardless of wealth, race, gender, disability, sexual orientation, gender identity, immigration status, or life circumstances, has meaningful access to justice. Throughout my career, both as an attorney and now as a judge, I have tried to use my position to expand access to the legal system, strengthen public confidence in our courts, and support communities that have historically been underserved or marginalized.
Inside the courtroom, that means ensuring that every litigant is treated with dignity and respect, that language access and interpreter services are readily available, that victims and defendants alike understand the proceedings, and that decisions are based solely on the law and the evidence. Particularly in the Domestic Violence Division, I recognize that many of the people who appear before the court are navigating trauma, financial hardship, housing instability, immigration concerns, or mental health challenges. My responsibility is to ensure that justice is not determined by a person's resources or ability to navigate an unfamiliar legal system.
Access to justice also requires accessibility beyond traditional business hours. The Domestic Violence Courthouse has developed a unique after-hours emergency process unlike any other courthouse in the country. Through a rotating judicial assignment, judges are available to review emergency petitions and issue Orders of Protection well beyond normal court hours, including evenings, weekends, and holidays.
This system is particularly important for self-represented litigants. Individuals fleeing dangerous situations can seek emergency relief without having to appear in person. They may complete petitions online and appear remotely by Zoom, often late into the evening, or even at 2:00 a.m.. For many, this is the only practical way to access the courts, particularly those who are working, lack childcare, have limited transportation, or cannot safely return to court during regular business hours.
Throughout my time on the bench, I have proudly served in this rotation, reviewing emergency petitions and issuing Orders of Protection whenever immediate judicial intervention was required. For victims seeking protection from abuse, danger does not adhere to a court schedule. I have always viewed this responsibility as an essential part of judicial service, ensuring that the protections afforded by the law are available when they are needed most, not merely when the courthouse doors are open.
That commitment extends to the everyday practices that communicate respect and fairness in a courtroom. I make every effort to pronounce names correctly, to address individuals by their preferred names and pronouns when appropriate, and to ensure that everyone who appears before me feels recognized as an individual rather than simply another case on the docket. These may seem like small things, but they reinforce a fundamental principle of our justice system: every person deserves to be treated with dignity and respect. When people believe they have been seen, heard, and treated fairly, they are more likely to have confidence in the judicial process, regardless of the outcome of their case.
Outside the courtroom, I have sought opportunities to serve communities that have historically faced barriers to equal treatment under the law. 
Disability advocacy is incredibly important to me. I know that the American legal system has historically been slow to fully adapt to the needs of members of the disability community. I have been involved with The Chicago Lighthouse (Formerly: the Chicago Lighthouse for the Blind and Visually Impaired) for decades, beginning as one of the original members of its Junior Board. For the last approximately 15 years, I have served as Co-President of the Junior Board and serve on the organization's Board of Directors. In addition to helping organize fundraising and community events, I have volunteered as a reader for CRIS Radio, providing access to news and information for individuals who are blind or visually impaired, and provided outreach for the legal clinic that had been at the Lighthouse. My work with The Chicago Lighthouse has deepened my appreciation for the importance of ensuring that our institutions, including our courts, remain accessible to everyone.
Since 2017, I have served on the Board of Directors of Bright Star Community Outreach, a nonprofit organization serving Chicago's Bronzeville community. Bright Star works to address systemic inequities through violence prevention initiatives, trauma-informed counseling, youth programming, educational opportunities, workforce development, and family support services. I have also served on the board of the Lynn Sage Cancer Research Foundation and the Trinity Irish Dance Company, organizations that reflect my belief that strong communities are built through sustained civic engagement.
I have also worked to support those who have served our country. As the founder of the multi-bar association Salute to Veterans in the Legal Profession program, I helped create an annual event recognizing members of the legal profession who served in the Armed Forces while raising funds for veterans' organizations, including the Veterans Treatment Courts. Those courts provide treatment, counseling, addiction recovery services, mentoring, and other critical resources to veterans whose service-related challenges have contributed to their involvement with the criminal justice system. It has been especially meaningful to support programs that recognize both accountability and rehabilitation.
 Advancing opportunities within the legal profession has also been a central focus of my service. I have served as President of the Decalogue Society of Lawyers and the North Suburban Bar Association and currently serve as Financial Secretary of the Women's Bar Association of Illinois, where I work to expand leadership opportunities for women and promote mentorship within the profession. I received their Mary Heftel Hooten Award in recognition of these efforts. I have mentored first-generation law students, participated as a mentor in the Cook County Judicial Mentoring Program, moderated continuing legal education programs on recognizing and addressing implicit bias, serve on the faculty of the Judicial College, and remain actively involved in organizations committed to increasing diversity within the bench and bar.
I have been an active member of the Lesbian and Gay Bar Association of Chicago (LAGBAC) before I joined the bench. Through that organization, I have mentored law students, participated on panels with various local law schools, including Northwestern University Pritzker School of Law, Chicago-Kent College of Law, and the University of Illinois Chicago School of Law, and spoken about improving the court system's response to domestic violence affecting LGBTQ+ individuals and worked to implement best practices in my own courtroom. I have been a supporter and volunteer with Rainbow Railroad, which helps LGBTQ+ refugees worldwide working to escape horrific oppression. Earlier in my career, as an Assistant State's Attorney, I also served on one of the nation's first specialized treatment calls for women and transgender individuals charged with nonviolent offenses, an innovative courtroom that sought to address the underlying issues contributing to repeated involvement with the criminal justice system by connecting participants with treatment, housing, employment, and other supportive services. That experience reinforced for me that equal justice requires understanding the unique barriers different communities face while applying the law fairly and consistently.
I have been humbled to receive awards from my work with the Diversity Scholarship Foundation; the “Justice Laura Liu Access to Justice Award” (2026) and the “Advocate for Diversity Award” (2022), as well  as the Building Bridges Award presented in tandem by the Arab American Bar Association and the Decalogue Society. While I am grateful for those recognitions, I view them not as accomplishments in themselves, but as reminders that promoting equal access to justice requires ongoing work.
 Whether presiding in a courtroom, mentoring future lawyers, supporting veterans, advocating for individuals with disabilities, or working alongside organizations that strengthen underserved communities, my goal has remained the same: to help ensure that our legal system is accessible, fair, and worthy of the public's trust for everyone it serves. I have worked throughout my career – in the community, the courtroom and the classroom – to encourage people of diverse backgrounds to enter the legal profession and excel in their careers. This is a foundational value for me.
