survey.q: Where did you grow up and how has your personal background influenced your practice of law?
survey.a:
I grew up in the working middle class Ashburn/Wrightwood community on the South Side of Chicago. I lived in Ashburn/Wrightwood until my early thirties when I lived on the North Side for a brief two-year period before returning to the South Side to start a family in Morgan Park.
I was born into a family of eight . Both my parents worked. My mother took in a foster child when she allowed my best friend to move in when his family became homeless. At that point we had ten people in our 1400 square foot house but we loved it.
As children we were encouraged to work and do volunteer work in the community. Both of my parents were active volunteers in Democratic politics and local community groups. As adults, all my siblings and  I also became active volunteers in Democratic politics and local groups. As children, our mothers cousin , Ald. (later Judge) James Murray , drafted and  sponsored the first Fair Housing Ordinance that passed   the Chicago City Council . We felt fiercely loyal to our neighborhood. 
I attended CPS Foster Park Elementary and St Thomas More grammar school. I attended Mt Carmel High School in Woodlawn and met kids from all over the South Side. Since 2022  ,I’ve chaired a weekly recovery meeting to assist at risk individuals, particularly younger adults with substance abuse issues at Mt. Carmel. I’ve done these things   because of the debt and loyalty I feel to the Mt. Carmel priests ,brothers and lay volunteers. I also do so out of loyalty to the kids who come from the South Side neighborhoods in which I reside and was raised. 
At Mt. Carmel, I was given Mercy when I deserved none and Justice when appropriate.   To that end , as a legal practitioner and on the bench, I attempt to temper any justice with mercy whenever possible. I’ve  always tried to give a second chance where appropriate and legally permissible .
As an attorney and as a judge I found that the individuals who were most likely to have success and avoid serious issues with the legal system had the following attributes: They were able to participate in team athletics or group activities involving teamwork : they were able to avoid substance abuse issues and they had good role models and mentors.  Those individuals who had that good fortune invariably attributed their success to coaches, mentors and volunteers.
To that end as both a judge and attorney, I sought to volunteer as a coach, mentor and community member. One of the reasons that I still seek to do so is so that the community can see a judge be an active part of the community.
I started by volunteering in my community. Since the 1990’s I have coached at  local schools such as St Thomas More, Christ the King, Evergreen Southwest. I have coached for more than 20 years in basketball, football and baseball. I have coached young people of all sexes and identifications. I was a troop volunteer for South Side Boy Scout Troop 508.
 
In the early 1990’s I was a tutor and coach in the Tom Dart/ Lemuel Austin Basketball League and Academic Excellence Program at Fernwood Park in the Roseland Community on the South Side.  Additionally, I have coached young men and women’s basketball  for the South Cook Jaguars from 2012- 2023. I have been fortunate to maintain ongoing relationships with hundreds of former players.
I have lectured and presented at law schools, specifically for retired Judge Sheila Murphy’s Restorative Justice seminar UIC -Kent Law. I have taught and lectured legal clubs at CPS grammar schools and several high schools. I have been a panelist and presenter at multiple Chicago Bar Association continuing education classes. 
I’ve also been a volunteer referral judge  for the Lawyers Assistance Program. I’ve also been trained in peer support and volunteered to participate in interventions for attorneys having addition or mental health issues.
Also, as a board member for an Ashburn/Wrightwood 12 Step Meeting Club, I was a part of a group that made certain that the meeting club remained in Ashburn/Wrightwood. I started attending as an attorney and continued in that role as a judge. When there was a move to attempt to relocate to the suburbs, our group ensured that the facility stayed in the neighborhood. Our group felt that abandoning our neighborhood would isolate the people most at risk and desert a neighborhood that sorely needed the facility-although the costs are greeter at our location. This location offers the advantage of 24 hour access, kitchen and increased social and networking opportunities.
As a South Sider and having attended Mt Carmel, I was fortunate to be taught the benefit in the participating in team athletics . I was taught to compete hard, be part of a team and be disciplined with consistent effort every day. I was grateful for the adults who volunteered their time. I saw how the kids who were fortunate to participate were less likely to be  involved in destructive activities. Even those who did slip and wound up on the wrong side of the law, had an established framework for recovery. To that end I saw the enhanced value of athletics as key for accumulating the skills and habits to successfully navigate the difficult road of life.
In the legal world, I saw that that those who were fortunate to have the opportunity to participate as part of a team , even though most did not excel athletically, avoided trouble the most. These benefits were available only because of the adults who volunteered. In order to give back, I’ve sought to volunteer where possible. I’ ve particularly looked to volunteer as an attorney, a mentor and a coach. The people I’ve assisted have been able to give back as well. I feel as a judge and as a practitioner one must be part of the efforts to make the community a better more enriching place.

survey.q: Judges hold enormous power over the lives of the people in their courtrooms. How have you grappled with judicial power in your time on the bench?
survey.a:
I recognize the enormous power that the office of judge confers upon me. As a judge for the State of Illinois I have a great responsibility to the people of the Sate whom I serve. I have a duty to have thorough knowledge of the law and to be prepared. Every decision that the court makes has an immense impact on the litigants and their families.
Given this combination of enormous power and responsibility, I also have a duty to have thorough knowledge of the law, to be respectful to all litigants, and to make certain that those who appear before me feel heard. To that end, I spend long hours preparing for cases and take many continuing education courses dealing with successful court management techniques and communication effectiveness courses. Additionally, I have taken numerous courses on recognizing implicit bias. The goal of these courses is to develop techniques and strategies to eliminate any subconscious bias issues in my decision making.
I spend a great deal of time explaining the law and the consequences to unrepresented parties. Often this extra care operates to the irritation of some attorneys. I feel that the extra time is beneficial to the court and process in that the participants understand the role of the judge in the case. Additionally, I find that the additional time and attention reduces the number of court outbursts which I find are often the result of frustration with a feeling that one’s view has not been heard. I preside in a decedent’s estate court where often the court navigates longstanding issues and claims of theft, embezzlement and conversion between family members. These proceedings can be contentious and the culmination of years of conflict.
In many cases, at least one party is not going to feel they have been successful as to every issue they sought. Although not everyone can win their case, the judge should endeavor to ensure that all parties feel they have been heard and respected. The court must rule based on the evidence and the law but the judge should treat all parties with compassion and respect. This requirement is paramount to our service as guardians of the public trust.

survey.q: As a judge, how have you worked, both inside and outside the courtroom, to address the ways that the legal system, historically and in the present, has worked in favor of those with money, power and resources and against those without?
survey.a:
As a judge I have worked diligently to address these issues. I was fortunate as an attorney to work for the legal service provider Chicago Volunteer Legal Services (CVLS) as a volunteer pro bono attorney. I was simply following the example taught to give back by my parents. I also represented numerous pro bono clients in the course of my private practice. 
 I volunteered at the Chicago Volunteer Legal Services from 2001-2007. I handled court cases for CVLS clients. I was privileged to apprentice under longtime legal stalwarts Meg Benson, Phil Mohr and Peter Ashmore . More recently I’ve been fortunate to work with Jamie Shlaefer. In addition to representing clients in court hearings, I volunteered as an interviewer and in house attorney at the downtown office on a weekly basis . In my private practice, I handled numerous pro bono cases. One of my former pro bono clients, who served a significant sentence in a State of Illinois detention facility now has his own business and is the President of a Treatment Center where he was once a patient. So I see first-hand where volunteering makes a difference. The young man in question has positively affected more people than I’ll ever meet, but he is evidentiary proof of the potential for exponential growth of goodwill based on one act of kindness
 
As an attorney, I saw first hand how CVLS positively impacted the families of those who were indigent but direly need legal services. I saw the hundreds of other attorneys also generously volunteered their time but I was also aware that many more were needed. 
As a judge I have made consistent efforts to address this shortage by advocating that attorneys engage in more volunteer pro bono service, particularly in the Probate division. I consistently ask that the Probate bar volunteer for CVLS organization, specifically for the PCAP ( Probate Court Assistance Program) program. I have spoken to the CBA Young Lawyers committees on Probate and the benefits of representing economically distressed individuals on a pro bono basis
The goal of the PCAP program is assist deserving needy families by representing these families when family homes are undergoing the decedent probate process. Quite often these homes are undergoing legal distress -such as foreclosure, code violations or real estate tax issues. Quite often these families are able to continue to reside in these homes and retain whatever generational wealth those homes contain due to the volunteer efforts of the Probate bar. I was honored to be named the 2025 Cook County Judicial honoree by CVLS in their 2025 Annual Court of Honor Awards for these humble efforts over the years. 
One of the other manners in which I have attempted to to assist the financially needy is in the area of equal address to assistance with drug and alchohol addiction. Quite often treatment services are more easily reached by those with financial resources. I have been active in ensuring local access to no/cost  alcohol/Drug addiction support meetings in my longtime South Side neighborhood of Ashburn/Wrightwood , an historically underserved and majority/minority community. Since 2017, I have been a president, a board member and a financial supporter of a Club which provides these meetings with a safe location in which to meet. I have been involved with the club starting in 1998. Due to the efforts of our club, we are able to host more than 70 of these meetings a month. I was part of a group of supporters who pooled their resources to prevent the club from being moved from the city to the suburbs.
This club has been in operation since the early 1990s. Most judges  and treatment moderators will accept the signature of the meeting chairpersons regarding the attendance of a member as proof of attending drug or alcohol education meetings. Other court mandated treatment and education often require financial resources must be paid for but our clubhouse is able to provide these education meetings for free. There is absolutely no requirement for financial contribution to attend, no questions asked. Often these meeting are the first step to recovery and reinstating drivers privileges, which greatly boosts employment opportunity. 
I have been  a board member (since 2018) , and financial supporter for Guildhaus , a men’s residential addiction  treatment facility in Blue Island, another underserved community. Guildhaus offers a structured supported  sober environment  with counseling . I also speak to the residents at some of their weekly meetings. The Guildhaus has also purchased a yet to open Woman’s residential treatment house ( Hopehaus) ,  only the second on the South Side. 
These facilities provide no or reduced cost residential treatment facility which can be crucial to allowing individuals to establish a foundation which can lead to disentanglement from the legal system and establishment of a new life. As both an attorney and a judge, I have focused my volunteer efforts on the recovery issues particularly because freedom from substance abuse is the single most important factor in avoiding incarceration and prospering in todays economy. The government effort have been too little ,too late but volunteers have made  a huge positive impact.
Finally, I have voluntarily served the Court system as part of former Chief Judge Timothy Evans and current Chief Judge Charley Beach’s Restorative Justice Initiative.  Prior to Covid, I administered a weekly in -person  alcohol /drug recovery meeting in the Lower level of the Daley Center. I provided the supplies, materials and refreshment at no cost to the County. The meetings were held on my own time .More recently, since 2024, I have operated a weekly Zoom recovery support meeting on my own time and at my own expense. I have taken my own vacation time and spoken to the young people who are enrolled in the Restorative Justice program on a voluntary basis to advertise this support meeting. 
As with all these meetings, attendance is absolutely voluntary and voluntary attendance correlates to later success. The fact that is not part of my job allows me to tackle the task with greater enthusiasm. 
Since this is a younger group, attendance is not what I would like, but non successful efforts with younger people often plant the seed for future recovery. Often living drug and alcohol free is a solution to some of the dysfunction that plagues some young people.   I am hopeful that these efforts have at least conveyed a glimpse of hope for a better life. 
While sobriety and learning life-navigation strategies is not a cure all for all society ills it does cure a lot of problems in many lives. Since it is the only field where I have a skill set to convey, substance abuse recovery is the field one that I put most efforts into in to level the playing field.

retain-gerardo-tristan-jr.notable:
In 2023, Tristan and a brother, Horacio, were sued by their parents’ caregiver, who alleged the brothers failed to pay her $240 for her last three days of work. The caregiver also alleged that on her last day of work, Tristan berated her and stopped her from leaving his parents’ home after he accused her of not feeding the elderly couple. The caregiver, who had worked for the Tristans for more than two years, according to the lawsuit, said that “fearing for her safety” she called Horacio, who eventually called the police on his brother. Horacio told the 911 operator that Tristan “was blocking her way out of the house, is angry and agitated, and seems intox,” according to dispatch records obtained by Injustice Watch through a public records request. When officers arrived, they observed Tristan’s parents in “good spirits/health and no apparent issues with their caretaking,” and officers “did not observe any signs of intoxication on Tristan,” according to a heavily redacted police report. The suit was settled in May 2024 for an undisclosed amount. The caregiver, through her attorney, declined to comment.

In an interview, Tristan denied that he was intoxicated or that he ever stopped the caregiver from leaving the house. “I just wanted an explanation of why my parents, who were in their 80s, were not fed, and that was her responsibility. That’s all,” he said. He acknowledged that he was angry but said he was not disrespectful. Tristan said he instructed his brother to pay the caregiver and he didn’t know she hadn’t been paid until he received a letter from the caregiver’s attorney.

Tristan is also the brother of Homero Tristan, a well-known Chicago lobbyist and founder of the Chicago Latino Public Affairs Committee. Homero’s law firm, Tristan & Cervantes, is a city contractor hired to [collect outstanding utility bills from Chicagoans](https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2025/01/24/brandon-johnson-campaign-contribution-chicago-latino-public-affairs-committee-illinois-elections-board). Both the political action committee and the law firm contributed to Gerardo Tristan’s 2020 run for judge.

survey.q: Where did you grow up and how has your personal background influenced your practice of law?
survey.a:
I grew up on the South Side of Chicago with my parents and three brothers.  I currently live in the south suburbs with my wife, a speech pathologist in the Chicago Public Schools, and our two children.  I obtained my bachelor’s degree from the University of Notre Dame and graduated from the Valparaiso University School of Law.  For sixteen years I worked for the Cook County State’s Attorney’s Office.  In 2017, I began working for the U.S. Department of Justice as the Division Counsel for the Drug Enforcement Administration, Chicago Field Division.  I remained in this role until 2019, when I was appointed to the bench by Justice P. Scott Neville, Jr. and elected to the position in 2020.   
	   Throughout my career, I have gained an appreciation for all aspects of the law and how it impacts all people’s lives.  In the various roles I have practiced, first as an advocate for Cook County, in an administrative and regulatory role with the federal government, and now as a judge, I have seen the profound impact a seemingly minor ruling can have on a person’s life.  I am mindful that every decision I make has real world consequences, and I make certain I receive as much information as possible to make these important decisions.

survey.q: Judges hold enormous power over the lives of the people in their courtrooms. How have you grappled with judicial power in your time on the bench?
survey.a:
In my time as a judge, I have learned that litigants are generally uncomfortable in a courtroom setting.  People do not aspire to appear in court, they are in court because they are either being charged with a crime, the victim of a crime, they are suing someone or they are being sued.  I attempt to make sure all litigants are at ease by explaining what the court is doing in a certain proceeding, making sure they understand the proceeding, and asking if they have any questions.   I realize everyone has lives they need to return to before and after court so I try to accommodate people by allowing them to appear over video-conference or taking their schedule into consideration for appearances that work for all parties.   
	     Ultimately, judges are public servants and I treat all litigants with the patience, dignity and respect that they deserve.  Because the courts are an adversarial process, litigants will not always be pleased with the results that take place. But if litigants feel they are being heard, that their position is being respected, and that the rulings that impact their lives are made with sincerity and an understanding of the gravity of the ruling, I believe that we have fulfilled our duties as a judge.

survey.q: As a judge, how have you worked, both inside and outside the courtroom, to address the ways that the legal system, historically and in the present, has worked in favor of those with money, power and resources and against those without?
survey.a:
The justice system should be available to all, not just those with the money to hire the top attorneys or to gain access to the law.  As an attorney, I volunteered with a friend and created the mock trial program at Saint Xavier University in Chicago.   We led a team of first-generation college students in mock trial competitions against teams from throughout the Midwest.  The program began as an extracurricular, but we developed it into a two semester, credit earning class.  I have spoken to grade school and high school students in Chicago and the suburbs about the law, the courts, and the legal process and the influence it can have on their daily lives.  Additionally, I have served as a judge in mock trial competitions at the grade school, high school and collegiate levels.   
	     While presiding over the Sixth District problem-solving courts (drug treatment court, veterans court, and mental health court), I have seen first-hand how people with limited resources are impacted by the courts.  The poorest communities in Cook County are located in the Sixth Municipal District, and our problem-solving court team which I lead strives to improve the lives of the participants of the programs.  We locate and coordinate treatment facilities and providers for participants, facilitate housing and therapy, and provide resources for job placement and training. We have also teamed up the paralegal program at a local college to provide pro bono services for participants who successfully complete the program to have their records sealed and expunged.

survey.q: Where did you grow up and how has your personal background influenced your practice of law?
survey.a:
I grew up in the Austin area of Chicago in a two flat located at 1717 North Parkside, Chicago, IL. We lived on the second floor and my first cousins lived on the first floor. Each floor had two bedrooms. I shared one of the bedrooms on the second floor with my four brothers. The bedroom had two double bunked beds. My father emigrated from Ireland and had a 7th grade education. My mother had a high school education. Never in my wildest dreams did I think I would become a CPA, a lawyer, a State Senator, and a Judge. My life experiences have taught me so much that has made me a better Judge. But the most important thing I’ve learned is to treat others like I, or my loved ones, would like to be treated.
 
My experience in the State Senate was especially enlightening, rewarding, fascinating, and challenging all at the same time. My experience in the Senate gave me the opportunity to meet people from every section of our state and exposed me to issues I would not have been exposed to but for my time in the Senate. Serving as Chairman of the Judiciary Committee and being a member of five other committees gave me the exposure to many people and many areas of the law which has made me a better judge. While in the Senate, I was the chief sponsor of approximately 170 bills covering various topics that were signed into law by three different governors.

survey.q: Judges hold enormous power over the lives of the people in their courtrooms. How have you grappled with judicial power in your time on the bench?
survey.a:
While a Judge does have enormous power over the lives of the litigants in their courtrooms, I believe it essential to remember where you came from and remember that the people that appear before you may be unfamiliar with the judicial process which could be an intimidating and frightening experience. 
 
I try and put myself in the shoes of the litigants that appear before me. I do my best to follow the law and explain it the best I can in terms that the average person can understand it. I also do my best to answer any questions that any of the participants in the courtroom may ask. 
 
I also give the attorneys the time they need to prepare their case, to present their direct and cross examinations and to listen to their arguments. In addition, I read the new opinions and orders that are issued by our Supreme Court and Appellate Courts on a daily basis in order to give the best and most thoughtful rulings on any pre-trial motions, trial issues or post-trial motions that are heard in my courtroom.  
 
I remember like it was yesterday what it was like being an assistant states attorney and a criminal defense attorney in private practice and appearing before many different judges. I do my best to ensure that all the people in my courtroom (from the clerk, the parties, the attorneys and anyone in between) are treated with respect and the dignity they deserve. I strive to have everyone that appears in my courtroom to leave my courtroom believing they were treated fairly and that the process was fair.
 
I also do a lot of self-reflection on my decisions made in court to make sure I’m making the best decisions and I also make appropriate modifications where necessary to do better in the future.

survey.q: As a judge, how have you worked, both inside and outside the courtroom, to address the ways that the legal system, historically and in the present, has worked in favor of those with money, power and resources and against those without?
survey.a: I’m assigned to the Juvenile Justice Division of Juvenile Court. 99.99% of the minors that appear before me are represented by assistant public defenders and are charged with criminal offenses. The kids that appear before me reside in the 3rd police district of Chicago which is located at 71st and Cottage Grove. While I know and understand that money, power and resources can and have affected the legal system, I think the best way to keep money and power out of the courtroom as a judge is to follow the law and rule on evidence and the law with compassion. To stay in tune with the many issues that affect the legal system, I maintain membership in the Illinois Judges Association and many (I believe 14) Bar Associations. I have also volunteered as a judge with the local law schools and law schools across the country in their mock trial competitions. I also volunteer my time at a local grade school where I have the kids participate in a mock bill and mock trial exercise. And finally, I was a member of a group that created the Illinois Redeploy Juvenile court pilot program which is designed as an alternative sentence to the Illinois Department of Juvenile Justice.

survey.q: Where did you grow up and how has your personal background influenced your practice of law?
survey.a: I grew up on the lower southside of Chicago in an area known as the low-end, specifically on 35th Street. Our little basement apartment sat on a small street in between Stateway Gardens and the Ida B. Wells public housing projects. I grew up in a loving home with both my parents and my older brother. We were poor and our economic struggles were extreme, but those humble beginnings were marked by experiences and lessons that made me who I am today, and proud of how I made it to where I am today. The path to this amazing office  was one adorned with humility, grace and tenacity. A path that taught me the importance and necessity of being ethical, having faith, believing in divine purpose, and always giving back and reaching back. These early life experiences prompted me to go into public service law to assure that poor people could also have access to justice.

survey.q: Judges hold enormous power over the lives of the people in their courtrooms. How have you grappled with judicial power in your time on the bench?
survey.a: Judges indeed hold enormous power over the lives of those who appear before us and those who work with us. Greater than power is, however, our responsibility to be patient, unbiased, attentive, compassionate and respectful. Guiding procedures in that framework has allowed me to make legal and just decisions, while exercising the necessary firmness to reflect the seriousness of the process.  I have found that exercising proper temperament, operating in integrity, and treating everyone with simple dignity and respect, creates an environment where litigants and lawyers respect me and my rulings, even when things don’t go as they would desire. Likewise, my staff also respects me and appreciates that I see the value in them, and recognize their partnership in helping me to run an effective courtroom.

survey.q: As a judge, how have you worked, both inside and outside the courtroom, to address the ways that the legal system, historically and in the present, has worked in favor of those with money, power and resources and against those without?
survey.a:
The IL Supreme Court and the Administrative Office of Illinois Courts have given great attention to our need to advance accessible, fair, responsive and inclusive courts. Illinois Judges recognize that all individuals - regardless of their economic status, language, disability, age or representation preference – should be able to meaningfully participate in the court process. In this framework, we work together to assure that everyone experiences equitable treatment throughout the justice system. 
Some measures that I personally practice on the bench within this framework includes (a) assuring that individuals who are incapable of appearing in person can access court via zoom, (b) for indigent individuals who are on pretrial release with conditions, assuring that they are informed of resources available through pretrial services for bus passes, (c) assuring that interpreters are present to assist individuals who have language barriers, at no cost to them, and (d)  assuring that standardized forms are printed in different languages. I also make it a priority to make my rulings clear, detailed and in plain language, allowing litigants to ask questions to assure that they leave court with an understanding and with confidence in the justice system. Off the bench, I mentor students and young lawyers, guiding them on their path to the bench, and emphasizing the necessity of a diversified bench, one reflective of the demographic and experiential makeup of the communities we serve: diverse races, cultures, ethnicities, gender, gender preferences, socio-economic backgrounds, professional backgrounds and more.  A diverse bench is essential to public trust and impartiality.

survey.q: Judges hold enormous power over the lives of the people in their courtrooms. How have you grappled with judicial power in your time on the bench?

I realize that the decisions I make on a daily basis have a great impact on peoples' lives, and the enormity of that responsibility is not lost on me.  I practice patience, freedom from bias and a commitment to equal justice.  In practicing those qualities, I strive to ensure that every litigant feels that they are treated fairly and with respect.

survey.q: Where did you grow up and how has your personal background influenced your practice of law?
survey.a: I grew up in Chicago on the northwest side until I reached junior high when my family moved to the northern suburbs. I am the daughter of Irish immigrants. My parents emigrated to Chicago in the 1960s with only a 4th grade education. I am a first generation American. I am blessed to come from an extremely large extended family comprised of hard-working individuals who provided wonderful examples and strong moral character. We were taught to respect all individuals and also help others whenever possible. We lived by the Golden Rule which was to treat others the way you would want to be treated. My parents and the majority of my extended family worked in the public sector in “blue collar” positions. I watched them work hard, long hours and on weekends, working more than one job at a time to provide for their growing families. My personal background has had a tremendous influence on my practice of law as I was drawn to public service from the beginning of my legal career. I spent the majority of my career as an Assistant State’s Attorney in the Labor and Employment Litigation Unit (“L & E Litigation Unit”) in the Civil Actions Bureau of the Office of the Cook County State’s Attorney. I was proud to be promoted to Deputy Supervisor and eventually Supervisor during my tenure in the L & E Litigation Unit. One of my proudest professional achievements was being elected Circuit Court Judge and bringing my record of public service to the bench.

survey.q: Judges hold enormous power over the lives of the people in their courtrooms. How have you grappled with judicial power in your time on the bench?
survey.a: There is no question that judges hold enormous power over the lives of the individuals who appear in their courtrooms. As a judge, I feel it is crucial that I am respectful to everyone and that I explain my decision-making so all litigants, especially self-represented litigants, can understand my responsibility and my obligation when ruling on contested issues before the bench. While a judge is barred from giving legal advice, I try to explain procedure to self-represented litigants when feasible so they can understand the proceedings. I remind myself daily that being in court can create high anxiety for any litigant and the courtroom process can be intimidating and overwhelming to the people appearing before me. I do not take the responsibility or power of my position lightly and I am humbled every day that I get to wear my robe and take the bench. I strive to make sound decisions that are supported by the facts and law and exercise reasonability when my discretion allows it. Finally, the judge truly sets the tone in the courtroom by the way the judge treats all courtroom partners (clerk, sheriff, official interpreters, court reports, law clerks, judicial externs, and coordinators) and participants (litigants and attorneys) and by the way the judge addresses unacceptable or abusive behavior of an attorney or litigant that is directed to courtroom partners and participants. survey.q: As a judge, how have you worked, both inside and outside the courtroom, to address the ways that the legal system, historically and in the present, has worked in favor of those with money, power and resources and against those without?
survey.a: As a judge inside the courtroom, I strive to treat each litigant and case equally regardless of whether the litigant has money, power, or extensive resources. I direct any self-represented litigant to agencies providing legal aid or resources so they can get their questions answered or obtain legal advice. I am assigned to the Domestic Relations Division and I regularly encounter litigants at a challenging or tumultuous time in their lives. I am obligated to follow the law but I also exercise compassion when feasible. As a judge, it is important that I treat all individuals with the same amount of respect regardless of their legal or monetary resources. I make a conscious effort not to treat the high-powered attorney from the big law firm any different than a self-represented litigant who may have a more meager income or even be receiving public assistance or a fee waiver. As a judge outside the courtroom, I teach my children the importance of respect for all individuals. I try to pass on the moral compass that I was taught as a child as well as a sense of fairness and the desire to volunteer or give back to those in need. I am a member of the Illinois Judges Association and several other bar associations with whom I volunteer as a judge for several mock trial events throughout the year. I also volunteer as judge in classrooms across Chicago to either read books to elementary students or give a lengthy and interactive presentation on the dangers of social media and the world wide web to junior high students.

The hearing, in late 2021, took place while the woman was in the Cook County Jail. According to the appellate court’s review of the transcripts, Smith said that she had repeatedly interrupted him during an off-the-record portion of the hearing.

He said he didn’t know at the time that Zoom had a feature that allowed the host to fully mute all participants. “I would have operated differently now that I’ve received the instruction from the appellate court,” he said.

survey.q: Where did you grow up and how has your personal background influenced your practice of law?
survey.a:
I was born in El Paso, Texas, before our family moved to Melrose Park, Illinois. As the oldest of three daughters, I grew up watching my mother, a single parent and small business owner, work seven days a week to give me and my sisters opportunities she never had. She taught us the values of hard work, resilience, education, and service to others.. From an early age, I served as my family's translator, helping relatives navigate schools, workplaces, and government agencies. Those experiences gave me firsthand insight into the barriers that many low-income and Spanish-speaking families face when seeking justice. I also witnessed how victims of crime were often treated differently because of their socioeconomic status, race, gender, or ethnicity. Those experiences instilled in me a deep belief that the justice system should treat every person with fairness, dignity, and respect.
	That belief inspired me to become an attorney and dedicate my career to public service. I served as a prosecutor with the Cook County State's Attorney's Office for 20 years, advocating for victims, holding offenders accountable, and working to strengthen the communities I served. As a Felony Trial Division Wing Supervisor, I led and mentored a team of 18 felony trial prosecutors, ensuring that every case was handled ethically, fairly, and with integrity from assignment through disposition. Leadership in that role reinforced my belief that justice requires not only legal knowledge, but sound judgment, compassion, and an unwavering commitment to fairness.
	Today, those same principles guide my work as a judge. My personal background and professional experience have shaped my belief that every person who enters a courtroom deserves to be heard, treated with respect, and provided equal justice under the law. I strive every day to administer the law fairly, impartially, and with the compassion that my own life experiences have taught me is essential to public trust in our justice system.

survey.q: Judges hold enormous power over the lives of the people in their courtrooms. How have you grappled with judicial power in your time on the bench?
survey.a:
Judicial authority is a profound responsibility—one that I never take for granted. Every decision I make has the potential to affect someone's life, family, or future. That awareness guides me every day and reminds me that the privilege of serving as a judge requires humility, fairness, and constant self-reflection.
	Over the past five and a half years on the bench, I have remained committed to upholding the rule of law while treating every person who enters my courtroom with dignity and respect. Whether someone appears before me as a victim, a defendant, or as a witness, each person deserves to be heard, treated fairly, and to have confidence that their case will be decided impartially and based on the law.
	I also believe that justice must be accessible. I have worked to maintain a courtroom that is efficient, transparent, and welcoming, ensuring that everyone—including self-represented litigants and members of immigrant communities—can meaningfully participate in the judicial process, whether appearing in person or remotely.
	Serving as a judge has reinforced the importance of self-awareness. I recognize that every courtroom presents difficult and emotional moments, and I make a conscious effort to approach those moments with patience, empathy, and professionalism. Outside the courtroom, I prioritize exercise, meditation, and spending time with my family and friends because those practices help me remain grounded, focused, and able to bring my best judgment to the bench each day.
	The most important exercise of judicial power is restraint—listening carefully, applying the law faithfully, and never forgetting that every person who appears before the court deserves fairness, respect, compassion, and equal justice under the law.

survey.q: As a judge, how have you worked, both inside and outside the courtroom, to address the ways that the legal system, historically and in the present, has worked in favor of those with money, power and resources and against those without?
survey.a:
_ _	I believe that access to justice extends beyond the courtroom. While a judge’s role is to apply the law fairly and impartially, I also believe judges have a responsibility to strengthen public trust, support opportunities for future generations, and help ensure that people from all backgrounds see the justice system as one that belongs to them.
	Mentorship and community engagement have been central to my work throughout my career. As an active member and Secretary of the Illinois Latino Judges Association, I have worked to strengthen connections within the Latino legal community and encourage the next generation of attorneys through mentorship and professional development. I have had the privilege of mentoring law students, young attorneys, and aspiring legal professionals through organizations including the Hispanic Lawyers Association of Illinois, the Diversity Scholarship Foundation, the Puerto Rican Bar Association, the Cook County State’s Attorney’s Office, and local schools throughout the community.
	I have also welcomed college interns and provided guidance on navigating the legal profession, because I know firsthand how important representation, encouragement, and access to mentors can be in shaping someone’s future. Throughout my career, I have sought to create opportunities for individuals like me who did not have a pathway into the legal field.
	Education and outreach are also important parts of my commitment to service. I have spoken with law students from Mexico about the United States criminal justice system, participated in legal education programs, and had the honor of speaking at the University of Chicago’s Women+ in Law event. I regularly serve as a judge for mock trial competitions at law schools, high schools, and grade schools throughout Illinois, encouraging students to explore the law and understand the importance of ethics, fairness, and public service.
	I volunteer with community organizations that provide food and resources to families in need. As a board member of the Community Memorial Foundation, I help review and approve grants that support long-term housing, mental health counseling, and essential services for individuals experiencing homelessness. I am also a participant in literacy initiatives that encourage young students to develop a love of reading. Through these efforts, I hope to strengthen the connection between the judiciary and the communities we serve.
	Ultimately, justice is served when every individual—regardless of their background or circumstances—feels respected, heard, and confident in the justice system. Through mentorship and community service, I have worked to expand opportunities, strengthen trust in the judiciary, and encourage future generations to pursue legal careers.

survey.q: Judges hold enormous power over the lives of the people in their courtrooms. How have you grappled with judicial power in your time on the bench?
survey.a: I take the responsibility to administer justice very seriously. My last five and one-half years as a judge has provided me with extensive experience working with self-represented litigants, especially in the Domestic Violence Court, as well as managing complex commercial disputes with private practitioners in the Law Division. In each case, the importance of allowing each litigant to have their day in court, express their positions, be heard, and make their record, is extremely important. Showing respect in both demeanor and in providing a basis for your ruling is very important, so those impacted by your decision understand why you are making your decision. Taking the necessary time to understand their positions is key, so your ruling fully addresses their most important concerns. Often, if litigants are struggling, some procedural guidance may be helpful, to point them in the right direction so they may be aware of opportunities available to address their needs. Knowing the Court is there to serve the public and their needs is crucial to the successful administration of justice.

survey.q: As a judge, how have you worked, both inside and outside the courtroom, to address the ways that the legal system, historically and in the present, has worked in favor of those with money, power and resources and against those without?

Treating all litigants equally, whether self-represented or not, is essential in the administration of justice. In my own experience, I have always strived to give equal time for litigants to submit their written briefs, express their arguments, and make their record. When personal or health conditions may impact a litigant’s ability to provide discovery or finish certain tasks, I take into consideration their efforts, and provide extra time as necessary, as long as no parties are prejudiced by such extensions. I also provide all self-represented litigants with the Illinois Court Help telephone number for any administrative assistance they may need, and am very open to allow appropriate Zoom appearances where in-person hearings may impose economic burdens on litigants.
 
Also, outside of the courtroom, even though I have moved to the Law Division, I continue to work with the Child Relief Expediter Program at the Domestic Violence Courthouse in Cook County. That program, which I found to be so important, assures mostly self-represented parents in a domestic dispute who have children together (who do not otherwise have a Domestic Relations case) can continue to be provided protection under protective orders while also receiving agreed upon assistance arranging enforceable visitation arrangements and counseling. This free program has single-handedly reduced violence in innumerable cases where there may be conflict between the parents, but each wishes the best for their children. Providing those services in conjunction with orders of protection has been so successful that it is now being emulated by out of state jurisdictions, and I am working to expand the program throughout Illinois through my positions as a Board member of both the Illinois Judges Association and the Illinois Judges Foundation.

survey.q: As a judge, how have you worked, both inside and outside the courtroom, to address the ways that the legal system, historically and in the present, has worked in favor of those with money, power and resources and against those without?

survey.q: Where did you grow up and how has your personal background influenced your practice of law?

survey.q: Judges hold enormous power over the lives of the people in their courtrooms. How have you grappled with judicial power in your time on the bench?

I serve in the domestic relations division which involves the allocation of parental responsibilities, spousal and child support, division of marital property and debt, and orders of protection.  It is a great responsibility to make decisions that affect people's lives. I consider all the aspects of a case, the circumstances of the parties, the effect of my decision on any children involved and the future economic consequences on the lives of the people involved. I am careful to consider my background as I make a decision:  the fact that I came from a functional family, that my father never came home drunk, that neither parent played psychological games on each other or their kids, that I have never had to sleep outside involuntarily, that bullets never fired in my neighborhood - in other words that I have lived for the most part a life of emotional relative economic privilege -  and I do my best to address and eliminate any preconceived concepts I may have. I make no decision until  I am satisfied that it is fair, consistent with existing law, and otherwise in the best possible interests of the parties. During the case I pay attention to the demeanor and testimony of litigants and their attorneys. I listen to them and interrupt them only for clarity. When I make a decision, I explain it. People need to know that they have been heard before I tell them what I decided.

survey.q: As a judge, how have you worked, both inside and outside the courtroom, to address the ways that the legal system, historically and in the present, has worked in favor of those with money, power and resources and against those without?

When one litigant has financial resources to pay for  legal services and the other does not, I order that the financially able one pays the other party's fees. survey.q: Where did you grow up and how has your personal background influenced your practice of law?
survey.a:
I grew up in a low-income housing project on Chicago's South Side. My mother was a single parent who worked hard to provide for our family, while my father struggled with addiction and was in and out of prison throughout much of my childhood. Those experiences exposed me at an early age to many of the same challenges faced by the children and families who now appear in my courtroom.
My background did not diminish my belief in the justice system, it strengthened my commitment to making it fair, respectful, and accessible to everyone. I understand that many people who come before the court are facing the most difficult moments of their lives. While I am obligated to apply the law impartially and without regard to a person's circumstances, my life experiences have taught me the importance of treating every individual with dignity, listening carefully, and ensuring that every person feels heard.
Those experiences ultimately inspired me to become a public defender and later a judge. They continue to remind me that justice requires not only fairness in outcome, but fairness in process. Every person who enters my courtroom deserves to know that they will be treated with respect, that the law will be applied equally, and that their case will be decided on the facts and the law and not on their background, income, or status.

survey.q: Judges hold enormous power over the lives of the people in their courtrooms. How have you grappled with judicial power in your time on the bench?
survey.a:
Serving as a judge has reinforced that judicial power is not about authority—it is about responsibility. Every decision I make has the potential to affect a person's liberty, family, or future, and I never lose sight of that.
I have approached this responsibility by preparing thoroughly, listening carefully to everyone who appears before me, and ensuring each person has a meaningful opportunity to be heard. I strive to make decisions based solely on the facts, the evidence, and the law, while treating every litigant with dignity and respect. Particularly in Juvenile Court, I recognize that many of the young people who appear before me are still developing and often face significant challenges. While I hold them accountable when appropriate, I also consider the long-term impact of my decisions and the opportunities for rehabilitation.
Ultimately, I believe judicial power is best exercised with humility, fairness, and integrity. My goal is that everyone who leaves my courtroom—regardless of the outcome—knows they were heard, treated respectfully, and received a fair and impartial hearing.

survey.q: As a judge, how have you worked, both inside and outside the courtroom, to address the ways that the legal system, historically and in the present, has worked in favor of those with money, power and resources and against those without?
survey.a:
Throughout my career, I have believed that justice should not depend on a person's income, influence, or access to resources. Before becoming a judge, I served as a public defender, representing individuals who often lacked the means to effectively navigate the legal system. That experience continues to shape my approach on the bench.
Inside the courtroom, I work to ensure that every person is treated with dignity and respect, has an opportunity to be heard, and receives a fair and impartial hearing regardless of their background or financial circumstances. I make decisions based on the law and the facts, not on who has the most resources or influence.
Outside the courtroom, I have contributed to judicial education by teaching and presenting on juvenile law and have participated in community outreach through schools, bar associations, and civic organizations. I believe judges have a responsibility not only to decide cases fairly, but also to help strengthen public confidence that our justice system is accessible, impartial, and works equally for everyone.

survey.q: Where did you grow up and how has your personal background influenced your practice of law?
survey.a:
I grew up in Wauwatosa, Wisconsin, in a close-knit working-class family that valued hard work, fairness and mindfulness of those less fortunate. My father worked in a factory and my mother was a key punch operator (before the digital age of computer)  and then, secretary.  
I was taught that goodness was measured by how you treat someone that cannot do you any good, that it was important to forgive and not let the sun go down on your anger, and to remember that everything looks different in the perspective of the morning light. 
In both my family of origin and my own family, consisting of my wife and four now-adult children, disputes could sometimes be robust but always resolved by respecting the dignity of each other, with no “cheap shots taken”. 
I think these things have helped me in both my practice of the law, and on the bench. In practice, while I, of course, tried to win for my client, I did my best from trying to destroy, disparage or humiliate others. I strove to behave civilly, as a loving family might in a dispute. 
On the bench, I think about how I would I want my children to be treated by a judge or arbitrator if they were in litigation.  And then treat the litigants in a similar way.
I learned to be mindful that the merits of the argument and temperament were both important. 
I decided to become a lawyer in high school after two experiences intertwined. A teacher suggested I enter a “mock trial” program conducted by Marquette University. At the same time, I was in the play, To Kill A Mockingbird At school. I learned that a legal career could provide a person the chance to help others while at the same time engaging in a challenging, interesting, meaningful and fully engaging pursuit combining intelligence, wit, performance, integrity and flexibility.

survey.q: Judges hold enormous power over the lives of the people in their courtrooms. How have you grappled with judicial power in your time on the bench?
survey.a:
I do several things to keep in mind the power I hold as a judge.  First**, **as alluded to in my answer to question 1, I am mindful of the fact that the litigants in front are individuals’ worth of respect and equal justice no different than those people I love the most – my family.  Seeing it that way helps me to not want to ever abuse my power. 
Second,  I have a sign in front of me that reminds me to refrain from any unkind or unnecessary thought and to listen more that speak. 
Third, I focus on treating ev eryone with respect, listening to everyone and ruling on the law and evidence.

survey.q: As a judge, how have you worked, both inside and outside the courtroom, to address the ways that the legal system, historically and in the present, has worked in favor of those with money, power and resources and against those without?
survey.a:
Understanding the reality of which your question speaks, I served 20 years on the board of the Cabrini Green Legal Aid Clinic. I also volunteered to represent clients in the clemency program. 
Power imbalance, of course, extends beyond the legal system. I have actively been involved in refugee and immigrant work for nearly 40 years, including serving on the advisory board of Chicago’s World Relief for more than a decade. I have helped support  families that fled from Cambodia’s “killing fields” that arrived in the early 1980s, including one father of 3 who needed help navigating the medical system for a severe kidney ailment,  housed a  family from Cameroon, Africa, for over a year in my own home and helped others from the middle east, Venezuela and Mexico. Most recently I helped shelter and support an Afghan family of six. 
As a practical matter, in court, the greatest learning curve for me, has not been the legal issues, after nearly 40 years of litigation experience, but how to best address the self-represented and others without resources or power.  
I cannot unfairly tip the scales on the merits in their favor. But I can realize more effort is necessary on my part to give them time to explain themselves in the best way they can. I cannot give advice, but I often take the opportunity, after asking if there is any objection by counsel on the other side (and there usually never is, in my experience) to providing information about general civil procedure requirements or mention resources they might refer to help them represent themselves better.

survey.q: Where did you grow up and how has your personal background influenced your practice of law?
survey.a:
I grew up in Chicago’s Little Village neighborhood. Living there taught me the value of hard work and the importance of always doing your best with a positive attitude, no matter your role. It also helped me understand the real challenges many people in the community face, like economic hardship, language barriers, and limited access to resources.

These experiences have shaped my work as a public defender, private attorney, legal aid lawyer, and now as a judge. In each role, I have learned how important it is to treat everyone with fairness, respect, and compassion. I am always reminded that every person in court is a human being whose life can be changed by the legal process.

survey.q: Judges hold enormous power over the lives of the people in their courtrooms. How have you grappled with judicial power in your time on the bench?
survey.a:
One of the first things I realized after taking the bench was that every decision I make has consequences for the people standing before me. Whether it involves housing, consumer debt, or a civil jury trial, my rulings can have a significant impact on someone's life or livelihood. I never lose sight of that responsibility.

Over time, I have come to believe that judicial power is best exercised by being fair, prepared, and transparent. Being prepared means taking the time to read the briefs, research the law, and carefully consider the facts before making a decision. Being fair means approaching every case with an open mind and deciding it solely on the law and the evidence. Being transparent means explaining my reasoning so the parties understand how I reached my decision, even if they disagree with the outcome. 

Even though the court system is an adversarial process, everyone still deserves to know that they were treated with respect and that their arguments were carefully considered.

survey.q: As a judge, how have you worked, both inside and outside the courtroom, to address the ways that the legal system, historically and in the present, has worked in favor of those with money, power and resources and against those without?
survey.a:
Throughout my legal career, I have believed that knowledge empowers people. As an attorney, my primary responsibility was to be a strong advocate when representing my clients. I also wanted for them to leave with a better understanding of the legal system so they could advocate for themselves long after my representation ended.

As a judge, my role is different. Every participant in the legal system has an important responsibility. My job is to manage an effective courtroom while also giving everyone the opportunity to be heard and maintaining fairness throughout the process. Attorneys have a duty to advocate for their clients. Clients have a responsibility to be engaged in their cases and work with their attorneys when they have one. Self-represented litigants have a responsibility to do their best in presenting their case in court and take advantage of the resources available to them.

People come to court with different experiences and different levels of understanding about the legal process. While I cannot advocate for either side, I can make sure that everyone is treated with dignity and respect, understands what is happening in the courtroom, and has the opportunity to be heard.

I have also tried to contribute outside the courtroom by mentoring attorneys and law students, participating in bar association programs, speaking on issues that assist attorneys in their roles and issues that affect self-represented litigants, and helping develop courtroom resources that promote consistency and fairness in the administration of justice.

A litigant's financial circumstances, position, or access to resources should never influence the outcome of a case. My responsibility is the same in every case: to apply the law fairly, remain well prepared, and be transparent in my decision-making. I believe those principles help ensure that every litigant receives equal access to justice.

The courts have also taken deliberate steps to make the legal system easier to navigate for all litigants. There are many resources available, including the Illinois Courts website, help desks staffed by legal aid organizations, and legal resource guides that identify organizations by case type and subject matter. Illinois Legal Aid Online is another valuable resource that provides step-by-step guidance for completing court forms and understanding legal procedures. These resources can help bridge the gap in access to justice by giving litigants the information and assistance they need to participate more effectively in their cases. The resources are there, but making them effective requires a collective effort from judges, attorneys, court staff, legal aid organizations, and community groups to ensure that all litigants know where to find them and how to use them.

judge-of-the-circuit-court-vacancy-of-co.notable:
Rice first ran for judge in the 15th subcircuit in 2018. She ran for judge countywide in 2024, but [was removed from the ballot](https://www.injusticewatch.org/judges/judicial-elections/2024/name-change-law-used-to-target-women-running-for-judge/) by the Cook County Electoral Board for failing to include her married name in her filing paperwork. Rice, who says she has always used her given name in her public life, was in the middle of divorce proceedings at the time in which the judge had already officially changed her last name back to “Rice.” The board stated that because the divorce wasn’t finalized she should have added her married name to her paperwork when she filed; the board’s decision was affirmed on appeal. In a [special concurrence](https://drive.google.com/file/d/1JA1oeNps38c4LjRH0S0DYEx4kmE2GEHW/view?usp=sharing), Appellate Judge Freddrenna Lyle noted the law, which was meant to hinder candidates who changed their names for electoral advantage, unfairly penalized women because “only female candidates find themselves in litigation about surnames.”

In 2021, Rice was found by a Cook County Electoral Board hearing officer to have engaged in a “pattern of fraud” while gathering petition signatures for her mother’s campaign for Chicago Heights Park District commissioner. The hearing officer found Rice exhibited “disregard for the integrity of the election process” in her testimony about her signature gathering and that it “could not be viewed as credible,” records show. Rice disputed the officer’s findings in an interview with Injustice Watch and maintained that she was cooperative and told the truth under oath. “The findings of the hearing officer are her findings and her thoughts, but I testified under oath telling the truth. … I did not collect any fraudulent signatures.” She added that she disputed the hearing officer’s “assumptions about my character.” The hearing officer struck 32 signatures collected by Rice; Rice’s mother did not choose to appeal the decision and was removed from the ballot.
judge-of-the-circuit-court-vacancy-of-co.surveyExcerpt: I understand that court decisions ripple far beyond the individual litigant. Families worry about paying judgments and the consequences of delinquency. Children struggle with their sense of self when parental relationships must be limited—even for safety reasons—and face obstacles in overcoming personal challenges. Families experience devastating social and economic loss when a parent faces incarceration after criminal conviction. My practice is grounded in the recognition that every person standing before the court carries with them a network of individuals—family members, dependents, and community—whose lives will be directly impacted by the court’s decisions.

Thedford is a past president of the Illinois Association of Criminal Defense Lawyers and a former board member of the National Association of Criminal Defense Lawyers. Voters may recognize him from his [television appearances](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=46h59NNyQQc) offering [commentary in high-profile cases](https://abc7chicago.com/post/anthony-alvarez-video-portage-park-chicago-police-shooting/10555640/). He represented the family of 19-year-old Calvin Cross, [who was shot and killed by Chicago police officers in 2011](https://chicago.suntimes.com/2019/10/23/20927630/police-shooting-calvin-cross-copa-reverses-ruling-officers-keep-jobs), in a lawsuit against the city. The city settled the case for $2 million. In 2021, Cook County officials considered him to lead the [public defender](#public-defender)’s office, the [Chicago Tribune reported](https://www.chicagotribune.com/2021/02/23/contenders-for-cook-county-public-defender-appointment-include-some-high-profile-names/).

Between 2011 and 2018, the state and federal governments filed liens against Thedford and his wife seeking to collect about $249,000 in unpaid taxes, interest, and penalties. In 2020, the couple declared bankruptcy and reported that they owed the IRS some $220,000 and owed the Illinois Department of Revenue about $10,000. The bankruptcy filing indicated they were paying the IRS about $1,500 per month. Tax debts generally cannot be wiped away through bankruptcy, and state and federal tax authorities declined to comment on any debts owed by Thedford and his wife.

Thedford told Injustice Watch his state debt had been resolved and he continues to pay the federal government, though he declined to say how much he still owes. He said he “will be able to wrap this up pretty soon.” Thedford said his debts ballooned after he and his wife bought a home and borrowed money to improve it shortly before the 2008 housing crisis tanked its value. He noted that the Illinois Supreme Court vetted him before appointing him to the bench. Circuit judges make a salary of $258,000 per year. Recently-retired Justice Mary Jane Theis, who backed his appointment, declined to comment through a spokesperson.

They, along with my parents, shaped my world view and imbued me with a sense of purpose and responsibility to do justice.

It’s not going to keep somebody hungry from stealing some food, or it’s not going to keep a mother who needs Similac for her baby from (stealing). How is that going to deflect any type of crime?” she said. “No, putting some money in the neighborhoods that are way underfunded and giving people something to look forward to is going to change it way more than anything.”

Shambley represented 20-year-old Paris Sadler, who was accused of shooting a Chicago police officer in 2012. The case [became controversial](https://www.cbsnews.com/chicago/news/paris-sadler-pleads-guilty-to-shooting-chicago-police-pfficer/) after a prosecutor was caught lying under oath in an evidentiary hearing, leading to his firing. Pedersen ran unsuccessfully for Kane County judge twice, in 2020 and 2022. In both races, Pedersen was “not recommended” by the Illinois State Bar Association, based on negative reviews from dozens of fellow attorneys. Following her second defeat, Pedersen moved into her mother’s house at the edge of the 13th subcircuit in Cook County. “There was no motivation on my part to move to my mother’s house to run in Cook County,” Pedersen told Injustice Watch in an interview. “My mom needed my help, I’m a single mom with my twin daughters, and it actually makes all the sense in the world for us four to be together.”

Pedersen has been charged with driving under the influence three times since 2004, court records show. In the first two cases, she ultimately pleaded guilty to a lesser charge of reckless driving. Her latest arrest came in September 2023, after police in Streamwood pulled her over around 2:30 a.m. for driving more than 30 miles above the speed limit, records show. The arresting officer reported that Pedersen had the smell of alcohol on her breath and showed signs of impairment. The DUI charge in that case was ultimately dismissed, and Pedersen successfully petitioned a Cook County judge to expunge it from her criminal record over the objections of the Cook County State’s Attorney’s Office, records show. “I’ve made mistakes in my life, but it doesn’t mean that I don’t pick myself back up and keep going because that’s the type of person I am, and I think that’s the type of person most people are, and that’s why I believe that people deserve second chances, and third chances, and maybe sometimes a fourth,” Pedersen said in an interview.

Starting in 2017, Pedersen has been listed in state business filings as president of her father’s landscaping company, which was sued in federal court over wage theft allegations in 2018 and 2019, court records show. The earlier lawsuit was settled for an undisclosed amount. The most recent lawsuit, which also named Pedersen as a defendant, was certified as a class-action suit and settled in 2020 for about $100,000. Pedersen said that her father runs the day-to-day operations and that she took the position to help the company handle its financial and legal dealings.
